automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Fresh-concrete field testing during a pour at an active construction site: obtain a representative sample from the truck chute (ASTM C172), run slump, air content, temperature and unit weight, cast and label a set of cylinders, place them in initial field curing, and log/report results to the inspector and engineer. Conditions: mud, weather, moving trucks and crews, layout differs every day.

In-situ density/compaction acceptance testing on earthwork, aggregate base or an HMA mat: walk designated test locations, seat and operate a nuclear density gauge (or sand cone), take moisture readings, compare to the Proctor/target density, judge pass/fail, direct rerolling, and write the daily field report. Conditions: open grading or paving site with active heavy equipment.

Laboratory strength testing of hardened concrete specimens: pull cylinders/cubes from moist curing at 7/28 days, measure weight and dimensions, cap or pad, load into the compression frame, break to failure, record load and fracture type, compute strength, flag low breaks and issue the report. Setting: an accredited materials laboratory with standard benches, curing tanks and a compression machine.

Laboratory soil specimen testing: receive and register bagged samples, split/quarter, oven-dry for moisture content, run wash and dry sieve gradation, Atterberg limits, and standard/modified Proctor compaction curves (and occasional CBR), then compute and report classification and compaction targets. Setting: a soils laboratory.

Laboratory testing of aggregates and manufactured materials: aggregate sieve gradation, moisture/absorption and specific gravity; steel reinforcing bar tensile and bend tests on a universal testing machine; cement/mortar cube strength specimens. Setting: an accredited materials laboratory with standard test frames, ovens, balances and sieve shakers.

Laboratory asphalt mixture and binder testing: reheat and split a plant or roadway sample, burn off binder in an ignition oven for binder content, sieve the residue for gradation, compact specimens in a gyratory compactor, determine bulk and maximum specific gravity and air voids, and report against the job mix formula.

Detailed documentation of an existing structure at a project site: bridge, culvert headwall and wingwalls, retaining wall, tank, or building exterior. Capture dimensions and condition photographs, produce a measured 3D model or sketch for the designer; often over water, live traffic, or at height.

Existing-conditions survey inside an institution-controlled facility for a retrofit or expansion project: water treatment plant, industrial plant, campus building, transit station. instances.label: Assembling a prototype or low-volume circuit board in an engineering lab/prototype shop: placing SMD and through-hole parts per the BOM and assembly drawing, soldering (iron, hot-air, or reflow oven), inspecting joints. Electrically testing assembled boards and subassemblies: powering up, probing test points/nets, running continuity, in-circuit and functional test sequences per the test procedure, and recording pass/fail results for engineering.

Building wiring and interconnect: cutting/stripping wire, crimping terminals and ferrules, labeling leads, making cable assemblies, and mounting and terminating devices in a control panel, chassis, or test fixture enclosure per a wiring diagram.

Bench rework where the defective part is already identified (from test data or an inspection report): desoldering the component, cleaning the pads, placing and soldering the replacement, and re-running the test to verify.

Open-ended bench troubleshooting of a failed unit with no known defect: reading schematics, probing with scope/DMM, forming and checking hypotheses, isolating the fault, then repairing (component swap, jumper, rework) and verifying.

On-site maintenance of installed circuitry and electronic equipment: opening control cabinets or racks on a plant floor or customer site, checking and replacing boards/modules/wiring, adjusting and re-testing the installed system in place.

instances.label: Bench rework/modification of a PCB assembly to a specified change: implement an engineering change (swap R/C values, replace a QFP/BGA, add a component) or replace a part already identified as defective by test — desolder, remove residual solder, place and reflow the replacement, inspect. Occurs at an engineering lab or production-support bench with the board handled loose.

Diagnostic bench repair of a failed board or assembly with an unknown fault: read the schematic, power it up, probe with DMM/oscilloscope/thermal camera, isolate the cause, then improvise the fix (bodge wire, cut trace, re-terminate a connector, replace a burnt part, reflow a cracked joint) and retest to spec. Lab or repair-shop bench.

Depot/shop repair of a complete electronic unit (bench instrument, power supply, avionics LRU, medical or industrial device): open the enclosure and fasteners, isolate the faulty board/cable/fan/supply, swap the module, reassemble, then run functional test and calibration before release. Shop with ESD benches and standard test gear.

In-situ maintenance/repair of installed electronic systems inside a plant, lab, or institutional facility: open control cabinets and equipment racks, troubleshoot drives, PLC I/O, relays, sensors and wiring with meters while partially energized, replace the failed device, land/re-terminate wires, and verify operation with production staff present.

Field service at customer or outdoor sites — cell sites and remote telemetry stations, vehicles/vessels, customer premises: variable layout and weather, cramped or elevated access, drive out with a parts kit, diagnose, replace or rewire electronics, and verify service restoration.

Routine hot-swap maintenance in a controlled equipment room/data center: monitoring flags a failed plug-in unit (disk, blade, line card, power module); locate it in the rack, pull and replace it, or re-patch a fiber/copper link, then confirm the system recognizes the new unit.

instances.label: Bench troubleshooting and repair in an engineering lab or repair shop: a prototype board, instrument, power supply, or returned assembly does not work. The technician powers it up, probes with DMM/oscilloscope against schematics, isolates the failed component or subassembly, desolders/replaces it or swaps a module, reassembles, retests, and orders the part from the manufacturer or distributor.

Production or test equipment on a manufacturing/plant floor: an automated test station, PLC/motor drive, control panel, sensor or wiring harness faults out and stops the line. The technician reads fault codes, traces power and I/O, checks fuses/relays/cables, swaps the failed card, drive, or sensor, verifies operation, and coordinates with the OEM for a spare or firmware.

In-service repair at an institutional customer site (hospital biomed/imaging room, telecom central office, data center, commercial building system, substation control house): diagnose the installed equipment in place under access and uptime constraints, escalate to the manufacturer's field representative for parts, warranty, or firmware, then install the replacement and verify performance.

Hard-to-reproduce or intermittent failure: repeated measurement sessions, data logging, thermal/vibration or stress testing, waveform capture, cross-referencing schematics, service bulletins and vendor applications engineers, then implementing the fix (component change, rework, firmware/ECO) and proving the fault is gone.

Field work at unstructured or outdoor sites: cell tower or remote pump/telemetry station, vessel, mine or construction site, or a small business/residential install. Layout differs site to site, weather and access vary, equipment is old or undocumented; technician diagnoses, obtains parts from the manufacturer, and repairs on site.

instances.label: R&D lab bench bring-up/debug of a new prototype board or subassembly: technician selects instruments (scope, power supply, function generator, DMM), rigs power and probes to arbitrary points on a one-off board, decides what to measure next as symptoms emerge, interprets waveforms and isolates the design or assembly fault.

Validation/characterization lab: running a defined, repeatable test sequence on a fixtured DUT (power-rail efficiency sweeps, RF S-parameter/parametric measurements, timing margining) with rack instruments, switch matrices and a test fixture; the plan and limits are pre-specified, results logged to a report.

Production test floor of an electronics plant: setting up and operating in-circuit, flying-probe or functional test on assembled PCBAs — loading boards, verifying fixture/probe contact and calibration, running the test program, logging pass/fail and diagnosing failing nodes for rework.

Component/device-level test: loading packaged parts into test sockets or wafers onto a probe station, contacting pads/leads, running parametric and functional test programs on ATE, binning/sorting parts and checking correlation and calibration.

Environmental / EMC / reliability qualification: instrumenting a DUT and installing it in a thermal chamber, burn-in rack or shielded/anechoic enclosure, running measurements over temperature or scanning emissions, and monitoring long unattended runs.

Field diagnostics of installed electronic systems (industrial control panel, telecom cabinet, substation relay rack, installed instrumentation): carrying portable test gear to the site, opening enclosures, connecting meters/analyzers to live equipment in a layout that varies site to site, and isolating the fault.

In a lab or integration bay, the technician integrates a prototype system into a chassis or rack: mounting PCBs, power supplies, fans and panel connectors, driving fasteners to torque, routing and dressing cable, mating connectors, then powering up and taking voltage/signal measurements.

At a bench in the lab or cable shop, the technician fabricates cable and wire-harness assemblies: measuring and cutting wire, stripping, crimping or soldering contacts, inserting contacts into connector housings, applying heat shrink and labels, and verifying with a continuity/hipot tester.

On site — a plant floor, an outdoor test stand, a vehicle or customer facility — the technician assembles and hooks up a prototype or test installation: mounting sensors/junction boxes on existing equipment, pulling and terminating field wiring in place, and verifying signals with a meter under as-found conditions.

instances.label: Panel shop / integration shop: assemble and wire a batch of repeat-design control panels from ECAD (EPLAN) data on a bench or assembly stand — mount DIN rails, ducts and standard components (terminal blocks, contactors, breakers, PLC racks) on the mounting plate, cut/strip/ferrule and label wires, route them in ducts and terminate at spring-cage or screw terminals, then continuity-check against the schematic.

Shop or engineering lab: build a one-off or highly customized control panel / test rig — cut enclosure openings for HMI and disconnects, mount a VFD with heat-sink clearance and shielded motor cable glands, mix components from several vendors, wire power and control sections, land field-device cables, then power up, load PLC/drive parameters and do point-to-point and functional checkout.

Field installation and commissioning inside a manufacturing plant: mount an enclosure/VFD/PLC panel on a wall, skid or machine frame, run conduit or wireway, pull and terminate power and control conductors at the MCC and motor, land I/O from sensors and actuators on the machine, then energize, set drive parameters, verify I/O and safety interlocks with an engineer.

Corrective maintenance on the production floor under downtime pressure: a machine or line has stopped: trace the control circuit against prints, apply LOTO, use a multimeter/clamp meter and PLC/drive diagnostics to isolate a failed relay, contactor, sensor, encoder, fuse, drive module or loose/chafed conductor in a crowded live cabinet, replace it, re-terminate, and restart and verify the sequence.

Scheduled preventive maintenance and testing of installed control equipment: de-energize and LOTO cabinets, thermal-scan and inspect panels, torque-check terminations, blow out/clean drive heat sinks and replace filters and fans, function-test E-stops, interlocks and safety relays, calibrate transmitters/loops, replace worn contactors and document results.

Retrofit/upgrade of legacy controls on existing equipment during a scheduled outage: remove an obsolete drive, relay logic or PLC from an installed cabinet, fit the new unit onto the existing backplate (drill/tap, adapt rails), re-terminate and re-label existing field wiring, download the converted program, and check out I/O and machine sequence before handback.

Through-hole and discrete part replacement at a bench: desolder a failed electrolytic capacitor, fuse holder, relay, potentiometer or multi-pin connector using a desoldering iron/vacuum or mini-wave, clear the plated barrels, insert and solder the new part, trim leads, verify continuity with a meter.

Swap of a designed-for-service plug-in module in rack-mounted equipment on a lab bench, test floor or data hall: locate the failed drive/card/power supply from indicators or logs, pull the hot-swap unit from its bay, insert the replacement, confirm the system recognizes it.

Internal part replacement inside an instrument, chassis or machine controller on the lab/production floor: remove cover screws, unplug ribbon and wire-harness connectors, unbolt and replace a defective PCB, fan or power supply, re-route cabling, reassemble and retest.

In-situ replacement in installed equipment at a plant, hospital or customer facility: technician works at an open control cabinet or machine frame, replaces a defective contactor, I/O card, sensor or terminal-block component with hand tools, lands wires, and verifies operation with precision instruments.

Replacement outside any controlled facility: electronics in vehicles, outdoor cabinets, towers, remote installations or a customer's premises/home — confined access, variable weather and lighting, tools and parts positioned ad hoc.

instances.label: Engineering lab bench: a prototype PCB fails a functional test. The technician probes with scope/DMM against the schematic, finds the cause, then modifies the board — swaps or re-values an SMD/through-hole part, adds an RC/filter cap, cuts a trace, installs a bodge wire — and re-tests until the deviation is corrected.

Lab/prototype shop: a prototype wiring harness, control cabinet, or electromechanical assembly misbehaves (mis-wired circuit, wrong relay/contactor, noise pickup). The technician removes and re-terminates wires, swaps a relay/connector/fuse, reroutes or shields a harness, and re-verifies continuity and function.

Bench adjustment of a prototype to bring measured performance into spec: turning trimmer pots, tuning screws on an RF filter/cavity, variable caps, or trimming resistive elements while watching instrument feedback (VNA, analyzer, meter) until the response meets the target.

Field or test-article modification: prototype electrical system installed in a vehicle, machine, outdoor test rig, or at a customer site. The technician diagnoses on-site with portable instruments and modifies wiring, sensors, grounding, or boards in cramped, uncontrolled conditions.

Pilot/lab area: an engineering change is already specified (e.g., replace U7/R12 with the corrected part on all units). The technician executes the specified component removal and re-soldering across a small batch of prototype boards and verifies each.
Pilot/lab area: an engineering change that requires wire adds, trace cuts, connector re-pinning, or added daughter-boards on a batch of prototype units, followed by verification.

tasks.label: Install or program computer hardware or machine or instrumentation software in microprocessor-based systems.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commissioning or modifying machine control software on the plant floor: technician connects a laptop to a PLC/HMI/motion or robot controller on an installed production machine, writes or edits the program, sets drive and axis parameters, jogs axes, forces and verifies I/O against field devices, and iterates until the machine runs to spec.

Installing or replacing computer hardware inside installed equipment at a plant or panel shop: mounting a PLC CPU and I/O modules, an industrial PC, a servo drive or communications card in a machine's control cabinet or 19-inch rack, landing wiring and connectors, powering up, loading firmware/parameters, and verifying operation.

Bench/staging preparation of standardized units: populating controllers or industrial PCs with boards/cards and loading firmware, OS or application images into batches of microprocessor-based devices, verifying each with a test fixture and labeling before deployment.

Engineering lab work on a prototype or test rig: installing DAQ/interface cards in a host PC, installing drivers and instrumentation software, wiring sensors and actuators to an embedded/microcontroller board, flashing firmware, and debugging the one-off setup against test equipment.

Field install or upgrade at a customer plant or remote asset (oil rig, wind farm, mobile or outdoor equipment): fitting controller hardware to existing, non-standard machinery, terminating field wiring, loading software/firmware, and configuring and verifying the system on site under as-found conditions.

sources.transferJustification: Cited to bound in-situ (E2) capability: general-purpose mobile manipulators working inside human work facilities are doing bulk material handling, not electro-mechanical hardware installation or controller programming.

tasks.label: Modify, maintain, or repair electrical, electronic, or mechanical components, equipment, or systems to ensure proper functioning.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Plant-floor corrective repair of installed automated production equipment (robotic cell, conveyor, packaging or process machine) after a downtime call: technician isolates/LOTOs the machine, troubleshoots drives, sensors, PLC I/O, pneumatics and mechanics, clears the jam or replaces/repairs the failed item in place, re-terminates wiring, and re-runs the machine to prove function. Access is cramped, faults differ every call.

Scheduled preventive maintenance and adjustment on installed electromechanical systems in a plant or facility: lubrication, belt/chain/bearing/filter replacement, torque checks on terminations, cleaning and re-seating connectors, sensor and axis calibration, alignment and backlash adjustment, ending with a functional check and PM sign-off.

Bench troubleshooting-and-repair of a faulty removed assembly of unknown fault (control board, servo drive, actuator module, instrument): technician uses meter/scope/test fixture to isolate the failure, decides repair vs. replace, performs the rework (desolder/replace parts, re-pin connectors, replace bearings/brushes), reassembles and re-tests to spec.

Shop/bench repair of a removed item where the defect and repair procedure are already defined and standardized: e.g., replacing a specific failed BGA/SMD device flagged by automated test on a known board type, or restoring a worn/damaged mechanical part (blade tip, seal or bearing surface) back to print dimensions and verifying it.

Modification/retrofit work in a lab or on a plant machine per an engineering change: fabricating and fitting brackets, mounting added sensors or actuators, rewiring/re-routing harnesses, integrating a new subsystem into an existing rig or prototype, then verifying operation with the engineer.

Field service on unmanned or remote equipment: repairing a UAV after a hard landing, servicing an ROV or a remote monitoring installation at an oil rig, crop field, rooftop or customer site, working outdoors with weather, awkward access and whatever tools and spares were carried in.

tasks.label: Inspect parts for surface defects.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench/QC-lab visual inspection of machined, cast or molded mechanical parts (housings, brackets, gears, seals) in a manufacturing shop: technician takes parts from a tote or tray, turns them under task lighting or a magnifier looking for scratches, burrs, dents, porosity, plating/coating flaws, and sorts accept/rework/reject with a written disposition.

Inspection of PCBs and electronic sub-assemblies at an ESD workstation or line-side station: checking solder joints, component placement, conformal coating, scratches, glue splash and contamination on boards of several product variants, flagging boards for rework.

In-process/first-article and sampling inspection of parts as they ... a production machine or automated cell (stampings, welded assemblies, painted or plated parts): pulling parts at intervals, checking surface finish, weld appearance, coating defects, and signalling the line when defects trend.

Walkdown inspection of installed machinery and components inside the plant: examining robot arms, conveyors, belts, gearboxes, piping, seals and frames for corrosion, cracking, wear, leaks and surface damage during a scheduled maintenance round, logging findings with photos.

Field inspection of large outdoor components/structures for surface defects (wind turbine blade erosion and cracks, tank or vessel shell corrosion, rig or building-mounted equipment), often reached by drone, lift or crawler, in weather and with site-to-site variation.

Inspection of prototype, one-off or very low-volume novel parts in an engineering/test lab, including fine detail under a stereo microscope: judging whether an unfamiliar surface condition on a first-of-its-kind part is a defect, with no golden samples or defect history available.

tasks.label: Install electrical or electronic parts and hardware in housings or assemblies, using soldering equipment and hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Repeat/batch build of a defined product subassembly in a manufacturing area: per documented work instructions, insert connectors/headers/odd-form parts into a board, solder the joints, then fasten the board and hardware (standoffs, inserts, covers) into its housing with hand tools; tens to hundreds of identical units of an already-released design.

Bench cable/harness and connector work: strip and tin leads, hand-solder wires to connector pins, terminal lugs and posts, seat contacts and hardware into connector housings/backshells, apply heat-shrink, verify continuity; wires and connectors of a defined build list.

One-off prototype or engineering build in an R&D lab or model shop: a novel design each time, built from a sketch, marked-up drawing or verbal direction - mount PCBs on standoffs, install panel-mount switches, LEDs, connectors and grommets in an enclosure, run and solder point-to-point wiring, dress and tie the harness, fit and trim as needed.

Rework, repair or retrofit of an existing unit: open the housing, locate the fault or engineering change, desolder and remove a failed component, wire or connector from a populated assembly, install the replacement part and hardware, clean the site, reassemble and retest.

On-site/field installation into equipment housings taken as found: adding or replacing a sensor, board, connector or cable inside a machine's control cabinet on a customer's floor, a vehicle, a UAV, or field/offshore equipment - confined access, soldering in place, no fixturing, variable lighting and posture.

tasks.label: Verify part dimensions or clearances to ensure conformance to specifications, using precision measuring instruments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench/metrology-room verification of machined or fabricated components (brackets, shafts, housings, prototype robot parts) against a drawing: technician takes parts from a tote or tray, selects calipers, micrometers, bore gauges, height gauge or runs a CMM program, checks the called-out dimensions and tolerances, and records pass/fail on an inspection report.

At-line/in-process dimensional check on the shop floor: technician pulls sample parts coming off a CNC, press, or automated production machine they maintain, measures key dimensions with hand gauges or a shop-floor comparative gauge, and confirms the equipment is still producing within spec (first-article and periodic sampling).

Clearance and fit verification on a subassembly being built or rebuilt in the shop: gear backlash with a dial indicator, bearing end-play/preload, shim thickness selection, shaft-to-bore fit, feeler-gauge gaps between mating parts of a gearbox, actuator, or mechatronic assembly on the bench or in a build fixture.

In-situ verification on installed automated equipment on a plant floor: measuring air gaps on motors/brakes/proximity sensors, conveyor and guide clearances, robot gearbox backlash, coupling/shaft alignment with dial indicators or laser alignment tools, and wear dimensions during maintenance or commissioning, working around and under the machine in place.

Field service call at a remote or outdoor installation (wind turbine nacelle, oil-rig equipment skid, water plant, hazardous-waste or infrastructure site): verifying wear dimensions and running clearances on installed electromechanical equipment with hand instruments under poor access, variable lighting, and no fixed layout.

sources.system: Robotic measurement cell (Mitutoyo CMM + handling robot, integrated by Engineering Data at Méca-Précis)

tasks.label: Fabricate or assemble mechanical, electrical, or electronic components or assemblies.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: One-off prototype/custom electromechanical build at an engineering lab or prototype-shop bench: from drawings or an engineer's sketch, mount motors, gearboxes, bearings, sensors and brackets on a frame, shim and align, torque fasteners, route and dress cabling; each unit is novel and built in a batch of one.

Electronic component assembly at an ESD bench or in an in-house electronics area: populating and soldering PCBs (SMT and through-hole), soldering leads to connectors and terminals, conformal coating and rework of small batches of boards for test fixtures and prototype units.

Cable and wire-harness fabrication: cutting wire to length, stripping, crimping terminals and ferrules, applying labels, inserting terminated leads into connector housings, bundling and continuity-testing harnesses for machines and test stands, in quantities from one to a few dozen.

Control panel / electrical enclosure build in a panel shop or shop-floor build area: machining enclosure cutouts, mounting DIN rail, wire duct, PLC, drives, contactors and terminal blocks on the backplane, wiring and terminating per schematic, labeling and point-to-point checkout.

Fabricating mechanical parts and fixtures in the machine/weld shop: milling, turning and drilling brackets, plates and shafts from stock, cutting and welding steel frames and guarding, deburring and fitting, typically batches of 1-100 pieces.

Repeat small-batch assembly of standard subassemblies or modules on a production floor: building tens to hundreds of identical actuator modules, sensor assemblies or machine sub-units to a defined work instruction, with screwdriving, press-fits, part placement and dispensing.

tasks.label: Align, fit, or assemble component parts, using hand or power tools, fixtures, templates, or microscopes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Repeat/batch build at a production bench or line station in a manufacturing facility: technician aligns and fits a defined electromechanical subassembly (housings, motors, brackets, bearings, boards) using jigs/fixtures, hand tools and powered torque drivers, to a released work instruction; the same part numbers recur across builds; output must pass torque/fit/QA checks.

Prototype, first-article or engineering-change build in an R&D or engineering lab: a novel one-off mechanism assembled from drawings and loose hardware, requiring trial fits, deburring, shimming, hole rework and iteration with the engineer; no established fixtures or sequence.

Build-up of units of a standard machine/drive product in a factory build area: mounting and bolting motors, gearboxes, bearings, actuators and covers to housings or frames with power tools and locating fixtures, repeated across identical units of the model.

Custom machine, test rig or automation cell build-up in an integration bay: fitting one-off frames, guarding, motors and drivetrains, then precision mechanical alignment of shafts, couplings, belts and rails using dial indicators, laser alignment tools and shims until runout/offset specs are met.

Microscope/ESD bench work on a defined product: aligning and fitting miniature precision components (fiber/optics, micro-connectors, small sensors, sub-millimeter mechanical parts) to micron-level tolerance with micropositioners, templates and bonding, verified optically.

On-site field work at a customer plant or installation site: fitting, aligning and assembling equipment components in place (mounting drives and sensors, aligning gearboxes and conveyor sections, reassembling a machine after repair) in a layout taken as found, with limited access and improvised support.

tasks.label: Develop, test, or program new robots.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: New robot cell/work-cell development and commissioning at a manufacturing plant or integrator's shop: mount the robot and end-of-arm tooling, wire and map I/O to PLC and peripherals, configure safety, teach and refine the motion program on the pendant, run dry cycles, and tune until the cell meets cycle time and part quality at run-off.

Prototype build-up and bench testing in an R&D lab: assemble a novel one-off mechanism from machined and printed parts, route and terminate wiring harnesses, solder and mount sensors, instrument the rig with DAQ/scope/load cells, run characterization tests, diagnose unexpected failures, and iterate hardware with engineers.

Control-software/firmware development with hardware in the loop: modify code, flash controllers, run the new robot on a test stand, tune servo gains and motion parameters, log and analyze data, reproduce and fix faults, document the build.

Field testing of new unmanned/mobile systems (UAV, AMR, UGV, ROV) at outdoor test sites, farms, or customer facilities: set up ground station and sensors, run mission trials, log telemetry, swap batteries and make between-run adjustments/repairs, and record results under changing weather and terrain.

Repetitive validation, burn-in and qualification testing of newly built robot units at a manufacturer's test area: unit fixtured on a purpose-built stand, run the automated functional/accuracy/endurance test sequence for many cycles, compare measurements against acceptance criteria, log pass/fail results.

Adjusting/regenerating the motion program of an already-installed robot in a fenced production cell for a new part or product variant: generate or touch up paths for the new geometry, verify the produced parts meet quality, and release the program for production.

tasks.label: Repair, rework, or calibrate hydraulic or pneumatic assemblies or systems to meet operational specifications or tolerances.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: On the plant floor, technician troubleshoots and repairs a pneumatic circuit on automated production equipment: finds a leaking or slow air cylinder, failed solenoid valve, cracked tubing or worn rod seal; isolates and locks out air, removes and replaces the component in cramped machine framing, re-tunes flow controls and cushions, and verifies cycle time and force against machine spec while production waits.

On-machine hydraulic repair inside the facility (press, injection molder, test rig, robotic positioner): replace failed hose, pump, filter or cartridge valve, contain and clean spilled oil, bleed air, then set relief/pilot/accumulator pressures with gauges to the documented specification and verify actuator speed and drift.

Bench rebuild of a removed hydraulic or pneumatic component in the maintenance/repair shop: disassemble a used cylinder, pump, or valve of uncertain internal condition, clean and inspect bores and spools for scoring, replace seal kit and worn parts, reassemble to torque spec, and functionally test on a stand.

Setting and calibrating a valve or regulator assembly to a pressure specification on a bench/test stand in a shop or production test area: mount the unit in a fixture, apply pressure/flow, adjust the setting (screw, shim, spring, or electronic trim) until cracking/opening pressure and leakage are within tolerance, then lock and record results.

Calibrating pneumatic instrumentation and control elements — I/P transducers, valve positioners, pressure switches and regulators — in an instrument shop or in place at the equipment: hook up a calibrator and air supply, run up/down points, make mechanical zero/span or nozzle/beam adjustments, verify hysteresis and repeatability, and complete calibration documentation.

Field service on mobile or outdoor equipment (agricultural/construction machinery, UAS or UGV ground-support gear, oil-rig or remote-site equipment): diagnose the hydraulic or pneumatic fault at the customer site with limited tooling, replace or rework the failed assembly, and recalibrate electro-hydraulic settings, working in weather, dirt, and awkward access.

It handles the same objects (valve bodies, O-rings, springs, adjustment screws) to the same pressure/leak tolerances a technician works to, but only with the work fixtured on pucks in a purpose-built cell, so it supports E1 only.

instances.label: Bench/lab assessment of a PCB assembly or electromechanical subassembly at an ESD workbench: technician selects DMM, oscilloscope, bench supply, LCR meter or functional test set, probes test points, powers the unit, compares readings to spec, and reports pass/fail plus fault location.

Scheduled condition-monitoring round across a facility: infrared thermography of motors, drives and panels; ultrasonic/acoustic checks for leaks and electrical discharge; vibration readings on pumps, bearings and gearboxes; reading local gauges and panel indicators; logging trends and raising work orders.

Acceptance/qualification test of a newly built or rebuilt system in a test cell or engineering lab: instrument the unit, run the documented test protocol (load, speed, temperature, electrical safety, HIL or dyno sequence), acquire and evaluate data, and issue a run-off report.

Field survey of a remote outdoor industrial asset owned by the employer (solar plant, tank farm, flare stack, substation yard, mine site) using a UAV or ground robot with thermal/visual payload to record condition data for assessment.

Hands-on field service diagnostics at a customer or remote site (wind turbine nacelle, packaging line in another company's plant, irrigation or farm machinery controller): unfamiliar layout, meter and laptop diagnostics inside a control cabinet, ad-hoc access and lighting.

tasks.label: Operate, test, or maintain robotic equipment used for green production applications, such as waste-to-energy conversion systems, minimization of material waste, or replacement of human operators in dangerous work environments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Scheduled preventive maintenance and breakdown repair on robotic sorting/handling equipment at a materials recovery facility or waste-to-energy plant: lock out the line, swap worn suction cups, grippers and pneumatic valves, clean camera optics and lighting, grease drives, replace failed sensors/cables, read controller fault logs, meter out an electrical fault, re-master and return the unit to service. Dusty, noisy, wet plant floor with awkward access above conveyors.

Test, calibrate and commission robotic equipment: run acceptance and dry cycles on a new or rebuilt robotic cell used to cut material waste (robotic paint/dispense, laser cutting, nesting), verify I/O and safety interlocks and light curtains, touch up taught points and tool-center-point calibration, measure and log test results, sign off performance. Work done inside a de-energized fenced cell with a teach pendant and instruments.

Run an automated production cell whose purpose is minimizing material waste (robotic machine tending on a CNC/press, robotic cutting or nesting cell, robotic dispensing): stage stock in the fixtures/magazine, start and supervise the program through the shift, keep the cell cycling, replace consumables and clear the occasional mis-pick. Fenced cell inside a factory.

Operate hazardous-duty robotic equipment inside an industrial facility to replace human operators: run the waste-to-energy bunker crane through receiving, mixing and hopper-feeding cycles from the control room, or send a mobile inspection robot on its rounds through hazardous plant areas to capture thermal images, gas readings and gauge values and report anomalies. Institution-controlled plant with fixed layout.

Operate unmanned aerial equipment over an outdoor, non-standardized site: survey a landfill, solar field, transmission corridor or storm-damaged infrastructure, fly the planned route, capture imagery/thermal data, and deliver the inspection record. Weather, terrain and obstacles vary site to site.

Deploy and operate a ground robot into a degraded or contaminated unstructured space (legacy nuclear cell, collapsed/flooded process area, spill site) to characterize conditions or retrieve/manipulate unknown debris, working around cables, rubble and unmapped obstacles.

tasks.label: Determine whether selected electromechanical components comply with environmental standards and regulations.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Desk-based compliance determination from documentation: for selected components on a BOM, the technician pulls supplier RoHS/REACH/WEEE declarations, IPC-1752A material declarations, SDSs and certificates of conformity, chases suppliers for missing data, resolves exemption claims, and records the compliance decision in the product/compliance database. Office cubicle; no test equipment.

Bench screening for restricted substances: in an in-house QA lab, the technician places selected parts (connector housings, plated contacts, solder joints, wire insulation, magnet assemblies) on a benchtop XRF stage or uses a handheld analyzer, chooses measurement spots on each distinct material, runs measurements, compares readings to RoHS/ELV thresholds, and flags pass/fail/inconclusive parts for further testing.

Destructive verification: disassembling a selected electromechanical component (small motor, cable assembly, relay, PCB) into homogeneous materials — cutting plastics, stripping insulation, scraping plating, separating solder — weighing and prepping samples for wet chemistry/ICP-MS/GC-MS run in-house or sent to a contract lab, then judging the reported concentrations against regulatory limits.

Regulated performance / environmental-conditions testing: mounting the selected component on a test stand or in a chamber (motor efficiency per IEC 60034-30/DOE rules, standby power, IP ingress, temperature-humidity or thermal-cycle exposure per IEC 60068), running the standard-prescribed sequence, logging data, and issuing a pass/fail determination against the regulated limit. Company test lab with standard chambers and instruments.

On-site verification round in the plant, stockroom or customer facility: checking that selected installed or stocked components carry the required compliance markings and labels, and that regulated conditions around them (refrigerant/gas leakage, emissions, thermal anomalies, segregation of restricted-material stock) are within limits; recording findings and non-conformances.

instances.label: In-process / final inspection of parts and electromechanical assemblies on a manufacturing floor: measure critical dimensions with calipers, micrometers, gauges or a CMM, visually check solder joints, fasteners, wiring and finish against drawings and workmanship standards, record results in the QC record and tag/segregate nonconforming units.

Functional/electrical performance testing of assembled units at an end-of-line station or lab bench: mount the unit in a test fixture, connect harnesses/probes, run the test sequence (continuity, hipot, torque/speed, sensor output, burn-in), compare readings to spec limits, log the data and pass/fail the unit.

Calibration and verification of gauges, sensors, test stands and measuring instruments per the calibration program: run scheduled calibrations against reference standards, verify test stands with master/golden units, perform repeatability and measurement-system (gage R&R) checks, issue calibration records and labels.

Specifying and coordinating the quality program: writing/updating inspection plans, control plans, work instructions and sampling procedures, reviewing SPC charts and yield data, preparing for and supporting ISO 9001/AS9100 audits, driving corrective actions, and coordinating with engineering, production and suppliers. Desk and meeting work with occasional floor verification.

Field/on-site quality assurance of installed automated or electromechanical systems at a customer site or field installation: verify the installation against drawings, run commissioning/acceptance tests and safety-interlock checks, measure performance, troubleshoot deviations and sign off the acceptance documentation. Site layout and access differ every time.

Routine documented inspection rounds of in-service equipment at an industrial site (plant, substation, tank farm, solar/wind site): follow a fixed checklist of inspection points, read analog gauges and indicators, take thermal/visual/acoustic readings, photograph conditions and file the round report for the QA record.

instances.label: In the employer's in-house machine shop, machining an aluminum or steel housing/mounting fixture for a servo or sensor assembly on a CNC mill or lathe: stock loaded and clamped, program run, part deburred and inspected to drawing tolerances (~±0.005 in) before release to the build.

One-off bracket, adapter plate, spacer or simple jig made on conventional equipment (Bridgeport-type mill, engine lathe, drill press) from a sketch or marked-out layout: clamp in vise, drill/bore/tap, mill to size, break edges. Single piece, needed same day for a test rig.

Sheet-metal housing or enclosure panels for a control box or robot-cell guard: blanks cut (shear/laser/punch) with cutouts for connectors, then bent on a press brake to form the box, deburred and checked for fit. Small batch, drawing-driven.

Stock preparation and secondary metalworking: sawing bar, plate or aluminum extrusion to length for frames and fittings, facing/chamfering, drilling and tapping mounting holes, grinding welds or edges flush.

Modifying or repairing an existing fixture, fitting or weldment: adding a welded tab or boss, re-drilling/enlarging holes to a new hole pattern, grinding the weld flush, so a damaged or redesigned fixture returns to service.

instances.label: Engineering lab / prototype shop: technician builds a one-off electromechanical prototype or test rig from the engineer's CAD drawings, sketches and BOM - cuts/drills brackets, mounts motors, gearboxes, linear stages and sensors, torques fasteners, aligns couplings, routes and terminates wiring, then powers it up and verifies against the engineer's intent, absorbing mid-build design changes.

Panel shop / lab bench: wiring of a control-panel mounting plate or DIN-rail assembly to the engineer's ECAD schematic - conductors cut, stripped, ferruled, labeled, routed in duct and landed on the terminals of already-mounted devices, then point-to-point verified.

Panel shop: complete enclosure build for a new design - lay out and machine the backplate, cut and mount DIN rail and wire duct, mount PLC, drives, contactors, breakers and terminal blocks, wire and label, fit door devices and glands, then continuity/insulation check and hand off to the engineer.

Operating factory floor: install and hook up a new machine, conveyor or robotic cell designed by the engineer - position and level the equipment, anchor it, mount guarding, photo-eyes and limit switches, run cable tray/conduit, pull and land power and I/O wiring, and assist the engineer at first power-up.

Plant floor or lab: commissioning, debug and design iteration with the engineer - run the new system, reposition sensors and mechanical stops, tune servo/drive parameters, rework wiring and swap components, take meter/scope measurements, and redline drawings as the design changes.

Customer site, outdoor or partially built facility (water plant, remote skid, retrofit in an old building, test site): install and connect an electromechanical assembly designed by the engineer, working off ladders/lifts with ad hoc fabrication, unknown existing structures and no fixed layout.

tasks.label: Make repairs to robots or peripheral equipment, such as replacement of defective circuit boards, sensors, controllers, encoders, or servomotors.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Plant floor, fenced production cell: an articulated industrial robot faults out on a joint. After lockout/tagout the technician supports the axis, removes the motor cover and bolts, disconnects power/brake/encoder connectors, extracts the failed servomotor or joint encoder (often with grease, seals, taper fits), installs the replacement, re-torques, then re-masters/zeroes the axis and test-runs the program.

Robot controller or electrical cabinet at the machine: technician de-energizes, opens the cabinet, identifies the failed servo amplifier, I/O or CPU board, power supply or fuse, unplugs ribbon/terminal-block/harness connectors, unbolts or unclips the board with ESD precautions, installs the spare, restores parameters/backup and powers up to verify fault clearance.

Peripheral equipment on the automated line: replacing a failed photo-eye or proximity sensor, conveyor encoder, vision camera, safety scanner, or damaged end-of-arm tooling component. Work is done in cramped or awkward mounting positions, followed by mechanical alignment, sensing-distance adjustment or camera re-calibration and a functional run-off.

Maintenance shop / depot bench: a failed unit (servo drive, gripper, sensor head, motor, controller module) is brought to a workbench, opened with hand tools, the defective board or component swapped, reassembled and functionally tested on a bench fixture before being returned to stock as a spare.

Field service on mobile or service robots at customer sites — warehouse AMR aisles, agricultural robots in a field, hospital delivery robots, restaurant servers, food-processing washdown areas. The repair (drive module, battery, sensor pod, controller board) is done wherever the machine failed, with variable access, lighting, and clutter.

sources.system: ALOHA Unleashed (ALOHA 2 bimanual workcell, Diffusion Policy)
sources.title: ALOHA Unleashed: A Simple Recipe for Robot Dexterity (arXiv:2410.13126)
sources.claim: Google DeepMind/Stanford's ALOHA Unleashed trained fully autonomous bimanual policies on a tabletop ALOHA 2 workcell, including a 'robot finger replacement' task (remove a finger from a slotted mechanism, ... and reorient a spare, precise insertion), achieving 75% success over 20 trials.
sources.transferJustification: This is the closest published analogue to swapping a defective component on a robot. It transfers only weakly: the part is a small snap-in finger on a lab table with no fasteners, harness connectors, lockout, torque spec, or post-repair calibration, and the 75% success rate is far below the reliability an employer accepts from a technician.

tasks.label: Troubleshoot robotic systems, using knowledge of microprocessors, programmable controllers, electronics, circuit analysis, mechanics, sensor or feedback systems, hydraulics, or pneumatics.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production line down: an industrial robot cell in a manufacturing plant faults out (servo/encoder alarm, collision, gripper misfeed, vision fault). The technician goes to the stopped cell, reads controller alarms on the teach pendant, checks E-stops, safety circuit, cabling and connectors, jogs axes, swap-tests suspect parts, isolates the root cause and restores production under time pressure.

Controls troubleshooting on an installed machine: an intermittent I/O or feedback fault. The technician goes online with the PLC/robot controller in the control cabinet, monitors and forces logic, meters 24 V, continuity and signal at terminal blocks and drive terminals, checks sensor alignment and grounding/noise, traces wiring on schematics, and confirms the fix.

Hands-on mechanical/hydraulic/pneumatic fault isolation on installed equipment: gripper won't clamp, cylinder slow, hydraulic pressure sag, gearbox noise or excess backlash, belt slip. Technician gauges pressures, cycles valves manually, listens and feels, partially disassembles, measures play, and identifies the failed component.

Condition-monitoring diagnostic round over the plant's automated equipment: walk the lines looking for compressed-air leaks, overheating motors/drives, abnormal vibration or noise on rotating parts, and flag the degrading component so a work order can be raised. Fixed layout, plant-controlled premises.

Bench-level electrical fault isolation in the maintenance shop: a controller board, I/O card, sensor or cable harness removed from a robot is diagnosed on the bench with meter, scope and schematics to find the failed component or the open/short, then verified after repair.

Field service call at a customer site with unfamiliar, variable conditions (a packaging line in a small food plant, an AMR fleet in a leased warehouse, an ag or construction machine outdoors). Technician diagnoses across electrical, controls and mechanical domains with only the tools brought along.

tasks.label: Install, program, or repair programmable controllers, robot controllers, end-of-arm tools, or conveyors.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Install a programmable controller or robot controller: mount the enclosure/back-plate, snap PLC, I/O modules, breakers and terminal blocks onto DIN rail, cut ducts, land and label wires on terminals, then pull and terminate field cables to motors, sensors and the robot arm in a plant or panel shop.

Program or re-teach a robot controller for a new part, fixture or product changeover inside a fenced robot cell: create/modify the motion path, set frames and TCP, dry-run, tune speeds and verify part quality.

Write or modify PLC/HMI logic and configure devices during commissioning: edit ladder/structured text on a laptop at the panel, force and check I/O against field devices, verify interlocks and safety circuits, and hand over a working sequence.

Install, change or align end-of-arm tooling on an industrial robot in its cell: bolt a gripper/vacuum tool to the flange, connect air and signal lines, dress cables, set payload and TCP, and prove the pick.

Diagnose and repair failed hardware on a controller or end-of-arm tool: trace a fault to a servo amplifier, I/O card, power supply, encoder battery, solenoid valve or leaking vacuum cup; power down/lock out, swap the part in a cramped cabinet or on the arm, and re-commission.

Install, modify or repair conveyors in a factory or distribution center: mount or reposition sections and drives, replace belts, rollers, bearings, motors or photo-eyes, adjust tracking and tension, and return the line to production, often under time pressure amid running equipment.

tasks.label: Modify computer-controlled robot movements.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Touch-up of taught points in an existing production program on a fenced industrial arm (weld, dispense, machine-tend) after a fixture swap, tool change, or minor crash: technician jogs the arm with the teach pendant, re-records the affected positions and frames, and saves the revised program; deliverable is the corrected program in controller memory.

Adjusting motion parameters inside an existing program from the pendant/HMI or a laptop on the controller network — speeds, accelerations, corner rounding/blending, dwell, payload and inertia data, approach/retract offsets, interlock timing — to fix cycle time, path vibration, or a motion fault.

Revising or adding path segments for a new or changed part in offline programming/simulation software (RobotStudio, RoboDK, Delmia, Robotmaster), checking reach, singularities and collisions in the sim, post-processing and downloading the revised program to the cell controller.

Modifying the motion of a collaborative or small-batch robot (UR, Fanuc CRX, Doosan) via tablet/graphical interface or hand-guided waypoint recording, e.g. changing pick and place waypoints for a new tray or box pattern on a shop floor or lab bench.

Field-service or remote modification of robot motion at a customer site: editing waypoint routes, docking approaches or speed zones for warehouse AMRs, palletizers, or gantry systems, often over a VPN/remote session with a plant contact confirming behavior.

tasks.label: Perform preventive or corrective maintenance on robotic systems or components.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Scheduled preventive maintenance on articulated industrial arms inside fenced production cells (automotive/metal/plastics plant): lock out the cell, purge and refill gearbox grease/oil at each axis, replace controller backup batteries, inspect and re-dress cable harnesses and connectors, clean covers and fans, check backlash/repeatability and verify mastering, log results in the CMMS.

Corrective repair on the plant floor after a fault or crash: interpret controller alarms, troubleshoot to a failed item (servo motor, encoder, brake, cable harness, I/O board, worn gripper pads/vacuum cups, damaged dress pack), remove and replace it with hand and power tools, re-master/recalibrate the robot, dry-run and requalify the program before releasing to production.

Fleet maintenance of mobile robots and AGVs/AMRs in a warehouse or distribution center: pull a unit to the maintenance bay, swap drive units, casters/wheels and belts, replace or service batteries, clean and align lidar/camera/safety scanners, run diagnostics and a test drive, then return the unit to the floor while the fleet keeps running.

Consumable/tooling service on welding end-of-arm tooling in fenced production cells: dressing and replacing spot-weld electrode caps on servo guns per weld counts, and cleaning MIG torch nozzles, cutting wire and applying anti-spatter, with verification that the tooling is correctly seated before production resumes.

Bench-level rebuild of removed components in a service shop: disassemble a robot wrist or RV/harmonic gearbox, clean and inspect parts, replace bearings/seals/worn gears, reassemble to torque spec, and run it on a test stand before returning it to the plant.

Field service at varied customer or outdoor sites: travel to a small job shop, food plant, dairy with robotic milkers, or an agricultural/outdoor automated system; diagnose in place with limited access and no fixed layout, repair or replace components, and recommission the machine.

tasks.label: Align, fit, or assemble components, using hand tools, power tools, fixtures, templates, or microscopes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Small-batch/repeat build of standardized robotic units and subassemblies on a bench or short line at a robot OEM or integrator shop: pressing bearings, mating motors and gearboxes to housings, seating dowel pins, driving fasteners to torque with power drivers, using build fixtures and go/no-go templates. Same part number built many times; work instructions and fixtures already exist.

One-off build-up of custom end-of-arm tooling, jigs, fixtures and mounting brackets from machined plates, extrusion and catalog components (grippers, vacuum cups, pneumatics, proximity sensors): drilling and tapping, deburring, shimming to fit, bolting, squaring to the robot flange, checking with square and indicator, reworking until it fits. Each build is a new design.

On-site mechanical installation and alignment of robot cell hardware at a customer plant or in the shop's staging bay: setting and leveling robot pedestals, anchoring baseplates, aligning conveyors/feeders/tool stands to the robot, mounting and aiming photo-eyes, cameras and safety scanners, fitting guarding panels, shimming and dial-indicator/laser alignment, working around existing equipment and people.

Bench precision work under a stereo microscope in a lab or cleanroom: aligning and attaching optical/fiber and sensor elements, seating fine-pitch connectors and flex cables, fitting miniature actuator or encoder parts, using tweezers, micro-drivers and micropositioners with visual alignment to fiducials.

Prototype and R&D build-up in an engineering lab: assembling novel test rigs and experimental robot mechanisms from mixed printed, machined and off-the-shelf parts, interpreting incomplete drawings, trial-fitting, modifying parts, and iterating with the design engineer until the assembly functions.

tasks.label: Attach wires between controllers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Shop build of a new robot-cell control panel at an integrator/OEM: mounting plate or wiring frame on a bench, technician runs and lands the interconnecting conductors between the PLC, robot-controller interface module, servo drives, safety controller and terminal strips per the CAD wiring diagram — cut to length, strip, crimp ferrules, label, land in push-in or screw terminals, dress into wire ducts, tug/torque check.

On-site installation/commissioning at a customer plant: landing conductors between the robot controller and the cell PLC / safety controller inside the enclosures — new wires added to a freshly built cell, terminated on DIN-rail terminal blocks and controller I/O terminals at both ends, routed in the cabinet's ducts, per the drawing package.

On-site interconnect run between separate controller enclosures several meters apart: pulling a multiconductor control cable or prefabricated robot motor/encoder/EtherCAT cable through cable tray, conduit or a drag chain across the cell, glanding it into both cabinets, mating heavy circular/industrial connectors and terminating the loose ends, then continuity/ring-out check.

Maintenance, troubleshooting and rework in the field: a wire between controllers is broken, chafed, loose or mis-landed; the technician works inside an already densely populated live-adjacent cabinet during a short downtime window, traces the conductor, removes it from the bundle/duct, fabricates and lands a replacement alongside existing wiring, and re-tests.

Lab / prototype / educational bench: one-off wiring between motor controllers, microcontroller boards, drives and I/O boards on a test rig or prototype robot — small-gauge wire, crimped JST/Molex or soldered board-header connections, improvised routing, layout changing as the prototype evolves.

tasks.label: Evaluate the efficiency and reliability of industrial robotic systems, reprogramming or calibrating to achieve maximum quantity and quality.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: After a crash, gripper/tool swap, motor-reducer replacement or gradual drift, the technician re-establishes the robot's mastering, tool centre point and part/user frames on a fenced production cell (arc welding, dispensing, machine tending): mounts a pointer or uses a fixed datum, touches reference points, updates frames, runs a test part and confirms positions are back in tolerance before releasing the cell to production.

A vision-guided cell (bin picking, conveyor picking, screwdriving) shows falling pick success or placement offset. The technician checks and redoes the camera-to-robot hand-eye calibration with a calibration board, re-checks lighting/exposure and vision parameters, then verifies pick and placement rates over a run of parts.

Cycle-time tuning of a single robot inside its fenced cell: the technician reviews cycle times, then raises speeds/accelerations, smooths blends and reduces overshoot/vibration at process points, validating that weld/dispense/handling quality is held at the higher speed.

Line- or multi-robot-level throughput optimization on the plant floor: analyze station-by-station cycle and blocking/starving data, rebalance robot task allocation and interlocks between robots, retime conveyors/fixtures and part presentation with upstream and downstream equipment, then validate throughput over production shifts.

Reliability investigation of a cell with intermittent faults or unplanned downtime: pull controller fault logs and condition-monitoring data, walk the line, physically inspect gripper pads, cabling/dress-pack, fixtures, clamps and incoming part variation, determine the root cause, correct it by reprogramming or recalibrating (or flag mechanical maintenance), and confirm over subsequent shifts.

Absolute-accuracy calibration and qualification of a high-precision cell (robotic drilling, machining, additive, precision dispensing): run a measurement sequence with external metrology (laser tracker/photogrammetry), compute kinematic compensation, load it into the controller, and verify accuracy against reference poses/artefacts for an acceptance report.

instances.label: Bench test of a removed robotic subassembly at the shop electronics bench: servo drive, controller/axis board, safety relay module, teach pendant or sensor is powered on a test bench and checked against spec with a DMM, oscilloscope and LCR bridge (supply rails, ripple, encoder signal quality, component values), results recorded pass/fail.

Acceptance or end-of-line performance test of a newly built or rebuilt robotic assembly (joint module, actuator, robot arm, controller cabinet) at a fixtured test station on the build floor: the unit is mounted on the stand, run through a prescribed test cycle while voltages, currents, timing and motion parameters are measured and logged.

In-place electrical testing of an installed robot or automation cell on a customer/plant production floor: technician opens the controller cabinet, probes terminal blocks, drive backplanes and I/O with a meter, scopes encoder and fieldbus signals, clamps motor phase current while the cell cycles, to verify performance or localize an intermittent fault.

Field-service verification at a customer facility (warehouse, food plant, hospital, semiconductor fab, lab) after an install or repair: confirm the robotic system performs to spec using meters, scope traces and logged data, then sign off the acceptance sheet.

Instrument testing of robotic/automated equipment in an unstructured or outdoor setting: an agricultural harvesting robot, mining/construction automation, or an outdoor mobile robot is tested where it sits — battery and bus voltages, drive currents, sensor signal waveforms — under weather, dirt and variable access.

tasks.label: Assist engineers in the design, configuration, or application of robotic systems.

instances.label: Shop/lab prototype build for an engineer: mounting a robot arm and positioner to a base plate, fabricating and fitting brackets and end-of-arm tooling per the engineer's sketches/drawings, routing and landing cables in the control panel, then reworking the build as the design iterates. Integrator or OEM lab/shop floor; one-off work, incomplete drawings, frequent back-and-forth with the engineer.

Teaching/creating the motion program for a new part family in an existing single-application production cell (e.g., a welding or dispensing cell): loading a sample part, generating and touching up the path, running a first article and handing results to the engineer. Fenced cell on a fab-shop or plant floor.

General configuration and commissioning support: setting up the robot controller and network/fieldbus I/O, defining tool center points, payloads and user frames, configuring safety zones and grippers/sensors, loading engineer-supplied programs and tuning parameters on a new or modified system in the lab or at a customer plant.

Application trials and validation testing for engineering: setting up instrumented tests (dial indicators, force gauges, vision checks), running sample parts and endurance cycles, measuring cycle time and repeatability, noting anomalies and failures, and compiling data and reports back to the engineer. Lab or plant test area.

Desk-based design support: producing or revising CAD layouts and cell drawings, wiring schematics and BOMs, building offline simulations of reach and cycle time, marking up documentation and drafting operation/maintenance procedures for the engineer's review. Office workstation adjacent to the lab.

On-site application support at a customer or field location: surveying the intended install area, measuring existing equipment and utilities, setting up and running a feasibility demo on the customer's own parts, adapting to whatever site conditions are found, and reporting findings to the engineer. Site layout and conditions vary and are not kept to any standard.

tasks.label: Install new robotic systems in stationary positions or on tracks.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Install a new 6-axis industrial robot in a fixed position in a manufacturing cell: rig the 200–1,500 kg arm with hoist/forklift onto a pedestal or floor plate, drill and set/torque concrete anchors, shim and level to spec, set the controller cabinet, route and land motor/encoder cables, air and safety wiring, mount the end effector, then power up, master/calibrate and verify.

Install a robot on a 7th-axis linear track/gantry: set and shim/grout rail sections, laser-align and level rail to tight tolerance, mount rack and pinion, cable carrier/energy chain and limit switches, hoist the arm onto the carriage, torque fasteners, then travel, calibrate the external axis and verify repeatability.

Install a lightweight cobot or small robot on a machine frame, bench, cart or pedestal in a job shop, integrator build bay or engineering lab: fabricate/bolt a mounting plate, mount the arm, connect controller and teach pendant, wire I/O and gripper, and verify operation.

Install a robotic system into an existing production line during a plant shutdown retrofit: tight access around existing conveyors, columns and utilities, coordination with electricians and millwrights, mounting of guarding, light curtains and area scanners, and tie-in to line controls under time pressure.

Install a robotic system at a non-industrial or field end-user site (dairy barn robotic milker, food-service or retail robot, robot cell in a leased space under renovation, outdoor/agricultural installation): floors and structures as found, layout different at every site, utilities improvised, work alongside other trades.

Install a robot in a cleanroom, semiconductor fab or regulated lab: gowned entry and particulate/ESD protocol, mount a wafer- or sample-handling robot into a tool frame or on a lab-automation track, fine-align to teach points, connect umbilicals, then calibrate and qualify.

tasks.label: Program complex robotic systems, such as vision systems.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Teaching and coding a new part program for an existing industrial arm cell (pick/place or weld path): defining frames and TCP, entering or touching up waypoints via pendant/keyboard, writing motion and I/O logic, then dry-running and saving the program.

Configuring a machine-vision application: creating/training vision jobs (pattern-match, blob, caliper, OCR tools), setting thresholds and pass/fail criteria, running the hand-eye or base-eye calibration routine, and mapping vision offsets into the robot program.

Debugging and modifying existing robot/vision programs after faults or engineering changes: reading logs, editing routines, adjusting vision tolerances, revising PLC-robot handshakes, and revalidating on the running line.

Offline programming and simulation of a complex or multi-robot system (RobotStudio, RoboDK, Process Simulate): building the cell model, generating paths from CAD, checking reach and collisions, post-processing and downloading code.

Integrating and scripting new sensors/peripherals on a collaborative or mobile robot: writing Python/ROS or vendor-script drivers, configuring force/3D-camera parameters and safety-related settings, and validating behavior.

tasks.label: Develop robotic path motions to maximize efficiency, safety, and quality.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Plant-floor teach-pendant programming of a new motion path for an industrial arm (e.g., spot weld, dispense, or pick-and-place cell): jogging the robot to waypoints, recording positions, choosing motion types, blending radii and speeds, then dry-running at reduced speed and iterating until cycle time and quality targets are met. The deliverable is the stored robot program.

Offline programming from CAD in simulation software (RobotStudio, RoboDK, Process Simulate, FANUC ROBOGUIDE): building the path, checking reach, singularities and collisions, optimizing cycle time and approach angles, then post-processing and downloading the program to the controller for verification.

Optimizing an existing production path to fix a quality or throughput problem — trimming air-move time, adjusting acceleration/deceleration, re-touching waypoints after a fixture or tool change, or altering torch/gun angles to eliminate defects — and documenting the revised program.

Safety-driven path work: routing trajectories to stay inside safe zones and soft axis limits, avoiding pinch points and interference with other cell equipment, tuning speed-and-separation or power-and-force limits for a collaborative robot, and validating the motion during risk-assessment sign-off.

Path creation for a collaborative or light-duty robot in machine tending, lab, or packaging use, via hand-guided lead-through teaching and tablet/app-based waypoint editing, including setting payload, speeds and I/O interlocks so the routine runs unattended.

tasks.label: Fabricate housings, jigs, fittings, or fixtures, using metalworking machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: One-off small machined parts for a robot cell (sensor mounts, spacers, adapter plates, pneumatic fittings/blocks): technician saws bar or plate stock, sets workholding on a manual or CNC mill/lathe in the company tool room, drills/reams/taps, deburrs, and checks dimensions with calipers/gauges against a sketch or CAD model.

Sheet-metal housings, guards and enclosures: laser/shear cut blanks, punch holes, brake-bend to the flat pattern, deburr, insert hardware — done in the plant's fabrication shop for robot guarding panels and control/sensor housings.
Welded steel jigs, fixture weldments and frames: cut tube/angle/plate to length, fit and tack on a welding table, MIG/TIG weld the assembly, grind welds flat, in the shop's welding bay.

Larger CNC-machined fixture plates and tooling from a CAD model: CAM programming, stock and workholding setup, machining pockets/locating bores on a 3- or 5-axis mill, in-process probing/inspection, deburr and tap, in the CNC machine shop.

On-site rework during robot cell install/debug: an existing fixture, guard bracket or fitting doesn't fit; technician measures the mismatch at the cell, decides the modification, then cuts/drills/taps/welds (portable tools plus shop machines) and iteratively test-fits the modified part on the live cell until it locates the part correctly.

tasks.label: Train robots, using artificial intelligence software or interactive training techniques, to perform simple or complex tasks, such as designing and carrying out a series of iterative tests of chemical samples.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Plant or distribution-center floor: technician teaches an existing industrial arm or cobot a new material-handling job (bin picking, palletizing, machine tending, kitting) by jogging/hand-guiding waypoints, defining grasp poses and approach paths, then running iterative test cycles with real parts and adjusting until cycle time, reliability and no-damage criteria are met.

Fabrication shop or process line: technician teaches a robot a path-following process on variable parts (arc welding, sealing, dispensing, sanding), teaching seams/paths, tuning process parameters, and running iterative coupon/part trials with inspection until weld or bead quality is accepted.

Integrator lab or production cell: technician trains an AI perception/manipulation policy for a new item set or task - collecting demonstration or trial data on the real robot, running the training software, evaluating on held-out items, and iterating on data and parameters until pick/insert success rates meet spec.

Laboratory (pharma, materials, QC): technician sets up and trains a lab robot or mobile manipulator to run an experimental campaign on chemical samples - teaching deck/instrument positions and the handling protocol, then having the system design and carry out an iterative series of tests, with the technician validating results and refining.

Hospital, warehouse or hotel: technician commissions and 'teaches' a mobile robot or fleet the facility - building/annotating the map, teaching routes, waypoints, docking and elevator behaviors, tuning navigation and interaction parameters, and running iterative validation missions among staff and traffic.

Customer site or field setting taken as found (construction site, farm, outdoor yard, shop with nonstandard fixtures): technician trains or retrains a robot on site to as-found geometry, lighting and clutter, re-teaching poses, re-collecting data and re-validating behavior under conditions no institution keeps to a standard.

sources.system: Path Robotics AW-3 / AF-1 Robotic Welding Cells
sources.title: Path Robotics raises $100M to automate welding - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Path Robotics' AW-3 and AF-1 welding cells use AI and computer vision ... fit up and weld steel parts autonomously and are commercially deployed in fabrication shops in the U.S. and Canada, i.e., the machine produces the robot's motion program itself.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot path teaching for welding. The technician's output is a validated weld program; Path's system scans each part and generates and adapts the weld paths itself, delivering the same output without a human teaching-and-iteration step.

sources.system: Path Robotics Obsidian AI (AW-3 cell)
sources.title: Intelligent Welding Cells | Path Robotics
sources.claim: Path Robotics states its Obsidian AI adapts to every part with no programming, doing vision-driven seam finding and path ... in real time inside its welding cells.
sources.transferJustification: Same transfer as above: the seam-teaching and path-tuning work a technician would do iteratively is generated and corrected by the machine within a purpose-built cell.

sources.system: Mujin robot controller / Mujin OS

sources.claim: Mujin's robot controller / Mujin OS performs real-time perception and motion planning so industrial robots generate their own movements, eliminating conventional teaching and programming; it is sold and installed in warehouse and factory robot cells.

sources.transferJustification: This is the task's own example - designing and carrying out an iterative series of tests of chemical samples - performed by the machine, including the experiment-selection and refinement loop the technician would otherwise supply.

sources.system: Mobile robotic chemist

sources.claim: The Liverpool robotic chemist has humanoid dimensions and works ..., human-designed chemistry laboratory using the same instruments a human researcher uses, while deciding its own next experiments.
