instances.label: Instrument a prototype/development vehicle or powertrain in the engineering garage: mount and bond thermocouples, pressure transducers, accelerometers and strain gauges at engineer-specified points, mount a DAQ box and power supply, route/loom/secure custom wiring through the engine bay and cabin, splice or tap vehicle circuits and CAN, then verify every channel reads correctly.

Install a development engine, e-drive unit or other major assembly onto a dynamometer test stand or into a mule vehicle: hoist and align it, fit adapter/match plates and mounts, couple the driveshaft to the dyno, and connect fuel, coolant, oil, exhaust and electrical service interfaces so the article runs on the stand.

Install bolt-on / aftermarket hardware on a test vehicle for evaluation (exhaust system, intake, suspension or brake kit, wheels and tires, roof rack, hitch, cooling duct), aligning it to mounting points, torquing fasteners to spec and checking fit and clearance to surrounding parts.

Build up and install test equipment on a laboratory rig or in a test cell: bolt down fixtures, actuators, load cells and encoders, plumb hydraulic/pneumatic/coolant lines, wire sensors to conditioners and the DAQ cabinet, and dress/patch cabling so the rig interfaces correctly with the control system.

Install portable test equipment on vehicles at the proving ground, track paddock, or on-road/customer site: fit telemetry and GPS units, cameras, wheel force transducers or a driving robot, run temporary cabling and power, and reconfigure between runs, outdoors and under time pressure.

Load a component (damper, alternator, e-motor, injector, brake caliper) into a standardized bench test fixture and connect its mechanical, electrical and fluid interfaces before a repetitive high-mix test sequence.

tasks.label: Perform or execute manual or automated tests of automotive system or component performance, efficiency, or durability.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Prepare and instrument a test article before a test: hoist/roll a prototype engine, transmission, battery pack or vehicle into the cell, mount and align it on the dyno cart or rollers, connect fuel/coolant/exhaust/driveshafts or tie-downs and cooling fan, bond thermocouples and strain gauges, route bespoke harnesses to the data-acquisition rack, and leak/function check before starting the run. One-off prototype hardware, no two rigs alike.

Execute an automated drive-cycle test on a chassis or powertrain dynamometer (WLTP/FTP emissions, fuel economy, EV range, hot/cold climatic cell, dyno mileage accumulation) on a vehicle already installed and instrumented: follow the speed trace within tolerance, shift, brake, run soak/restart sequences and log data for the duration of the cycle.

Execute a bench or rig test of a component or subsystem already mounted in its fixture (seat ingress/egress and cushion durability, door/latch slam cycling, knuckle or control-arm fatigue, brake inertia dyno wear/fade schedule, switch and wiring endurance, material coupon strength): run the programmed load/cycle profile to completion, record force-travel and failure data, stop on limits.

Run vehicle-level tests at a company proving ground or test track: repeated laps of rough-road/pothole/washboard durability courses, misuse events, brake and acceleration performance runs, high-speed mileage accumulation - driving the prototype to a prescribed schedule and route while onboard instrumentation records, over long shifts and in harsh conditions.

Run tests on public roads and in real-world conditions: PEMS/real-driving-emissions routes, real-world fuel-economy and range drives, customer-correlation mileage accumulation in traffic, hot/cold ambient trips - driving a prototype over a prescribed route in mixed traffic while logging data and noting anomalies.

tasks.label: Maintain test equipment in operational condition by performing routine maintenance or making minor repairs or adjustments as needed.

instances.label: Scheduled preventive-maintenance round on engine/chassis dynamometer test-cell hardware in an OEM or supplier test lab: check and top coolant, oil and hydraulic fluids; inspect belts, hoses, couplings, shaft guards and mounts; clean or replace air/oil/water filters; lubricate bearings; check combustion-air and cooling conditioning units; torque loose fasteners; log the round and flag anything needing a bigger repair.

Calibration verification and adjustment of instrumentation in the lab: zero/span an emissions bench with cal gases, verify a torque flange or load cell against reference weights/master transducers, check thermocouples and pressure transducers, adjust trim pots or update calibration coefficients in the DAQ, re-tag equipment and file the calibration record.

Minor repairs to sensors, cabling and fixtures after a fault or intermittent signal: trace a noisy channel, replace a broken thermocouple or pressure sensor, re-crimp or solder a connector, repair a chafed harness on a test engine or instrumented vehicle, replace a leaking fitting or hose, then re-run a check to confirm the fix.

Swap a failed or consumable module in rack-mounted instrumentation identified by system diagnostics: pull and replace a DAQ card, signal-conditioning amplifier, power supply, cooling fan, sample-line filter or battery in a 19-inch instrument rack, reconnect the harness and verify channels come back online.

Maintain portable/field test equipment at the proving ground or during on-road testing: mount, clean and secure PEMS units, wheel-force transducers, GPS and data loggers on a test vehicle; replace batteries, filters, cables and mounts; resolve faults in a garage bay, at trackside or roadside in variable weather before the next run.

tasks.label: Analyze performance of vehicles or components that have been redesigned to increase fuel efficiency, such as camless or dual-clutch engines or alternative types of air-conditioning systems.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Powertrain lab: technician reduces and interprets engine-dynamometer data from a redesigned efficiency feature (camless/electrohydraulic valve actuation, cylinder deactivation, variable-compression, low-friction hardware) — builds BSFC maps, computes fuel-consumption deltas versus the baseline build, screens for instrumentation drift or invalid runs, and reports whether the redesign met its efficiency target.

Vehicle-level fuel economy analysis: technician processes chassis-dyno certification-style cycle data (FTP-75, HWFET, US06, SC03) for a vehicle carrying efficiency changes such as a dual-clutch transmission or new shift calibration — computes weighted city/highway fuel economy and CO2, checks drive-trace and emissions-bench validity, and compares results to program targets and the prior build.

Climate/HVAC analysis: technician evaluates data from climatic-chamber or wind-tunnel testing of an alternative air-conditioning system (electric compressor, R-1234yf or CO2 refrigerant, heat-pump loop) — correlates cabin cooldown and vent temperatures against compressor power draw and the resulting fuel-economy or range penalty, and summarizes the efficiency trade-off.

Field/fleet data analysis: technician pulls logged CAN, GPS and fuel-flow data from durability or real-world evaluation vehicles, computes real-world efficiency by duty cycle and ambient condition, separates driver and route effects from hardware effects, and flags calibration or hardware issues for the engineers.

Ad hoc analysis supporting engineers: technician investigates an anomalous or off-target result (unexpected fuel-consumption penalty, inconsistent repeat runs), checks sensor calibration records and test-cell corrections, runs quick comparative and statistical analyses, and presents charts and conclusions in a design or test review meeting.

tasks.label: Improve fuel efficiency by testing vehicles or components that use lighter materials, such as aluminum, magnesium alloy, or plastic.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Chassis-dynamometer fuel-economy/emissions comparison of a vehicle built with lightweight parts (aluminum closures, magnesium components, plastic panels): technician rolls the mule into the emissions test cell, ties it down on the rolls, connects CVS/exhaust hose, fuel-flow and CAN instrumentation and cooling fan, runs FTP/HWFET/WLTP cycles, validates traces and reports fuel-consumption deltas versus baseline.

Coupon-level characterization of candidate lightweight materials in the materials lab: machined aluminum, magnesium-alloy and plastic/composite specimens are measured, gripped in a universal testing machine and run through tensile, flexure, impact and hardness sequences; results tabulated into a property report used for part-substitution decisions.

Component/subsystem bench testing of a lightweight part (aluminum control arm or knuckle, magnesium bracket/cross-car beam, plastic intake manifold or oil pan): technician builds and aligns the fixture, mounts the part on a servo-hydraulic rig or spindle-coupled simulator, runs the road-load/fatigue schedule, monitors for cracks and stiffness loss, reports durability versus the steel baseline.

Building and instrumenting the test article in the prototype shop/garage: swapping steel parts for one-off lightweight prototypes on a test mule, checking fit, bonding strain gauges and thermocouples, routing sensor harnesses to the DAQ, corner-weighing and ballasting the vehicle, and fabricating brackets or adapters as needed.

Track/road testing at a proving ground: coastdown road-load determination (SAE J1263/J2263) and on-road fuel-economy or mileage-accumulation loops with the lightweighted vehicle, using GPS/PEMS instrumentation, repeated runs in both directions within weather windows, then data reduction to road-load coefficients and fuel-consumption results.

Prototype/test-vehicle build-up and instrumentation in a shop bay: install data-acquisition units, CAN loggers, GPS/IMU motion packs, cameras and extra sensors in a one-off vehicle; route and tape wiring through firewall and trim, splice/breakout connectors, mount brackets, then verify and calibrate channels. Layout differs vehicle to vehicle; tight, awkward access.

Proving-ground execution of ADAS/automated-driving scenario tests: position soft targets and target-carrying platforms, run the vehicle through prescribed AEB/lane-keeping/crossing maneuvers at set speeds with centimetre accuracy, synchronise vehicle and target, and capture the data set and pass/fail result for each run.

Vehicle-level test-cell work: run the vehicle on a chassis dynamometer or in a climatic chamber through standardized drive cycles (WLTP/FTP, EV range, thermal) to validate powertrain control, energy management and connected-vehicle functions; follow the driver trace within tolerance and log emissions/energy data over long repeated cycles.

Routine public-road data-collection / validation drives: drive a prescribed route or accumulate mileage in mixed traffic while telematics, V2X or ADAS logging equipment records data for later analysis; nothing unusual expected of the operator beyond normal driving and starting/stopping the log.

Public-road shakedown and troubleshooting drives with an immature prototype system: provoke specific conditions, judge subjective system behaviour, take over when the automatic control misbehaves, and pull over to diagnose, re-seat, reflash or reconfigure the equipment before continuing.

Build a one-off instrumentation electronics module: populate and solder a small signal-conditioning or breakout board, mount panel connectors, switches and the board into an enclosure, hand-wire and solder the internal loom, label the panel, and bench-test the finished unit against the spec.

Modify, repair or upgrade an existing piece of lab test equipment: retrofit added sensors or a new controller onto an aging rig, replace worn fixturing, re-route instrumentation, and re-calibrate/verify the equipment before returning it to service.

Instrument and Control Technician (I and C Tech)
roles.description: Execute or adapt procedures and techniques for calibrating measurement devices, by applying knowledge of measurement science, mathematics, physics, chemistry, and electronics, sometimes under the direction of engineering staff. Determine measurement standard suitability for calibrating measurement devices. May perform preventive maintenance on equipment. May perform corrective actions to address identified calibration problems.

tasks.label: Maintain or repair measurement devices or equipment used for calibration testing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Scheduled preventive maintenance in the calibration lab on reference standards and support equipment (deadweight testers, environmental chambers, comparators, CMMs, calibrators): inspect for wear/damage, wipe and oil artifacts, replace batteries, fuses, desiccant, filters, worn cables and connectors, lubricate and re-level mechanisms, then log the work in the maintenance system.

Batch cleaning/decontamination of precision hardware in the lab before and after use: gage blocks, plug and ring gauges, mass standards, probe hardware and fixtures presented in trays, run through solvent/ultrasonic cleaning and drying, then inspected and returned to storage.

Bench repair/refurbishment of mechanical and dimensional measuring instruments found out of tolerance or damaged (micrometers, calipers, dial indicators, torque wrenches, bourdon-tube pressure gauges): disassemble, clean, diagnose the fault, replace worn springs/anvils/seals/movements, lap and adjust, reassemble and verify against a standard.

Bench troubleshooting and repair of electronic test-and-measurement instruments and calibrators (DMMs, oscilloscopes, power supplies, signal generators, data loggers): open the enclosure, trace the fault with schematics and test gear, replace fuses, relays, connectors, boards or discrete components with soldering, reassemble and verify/re-calibrate.

Routine servicing of an installed in-line analytical measuring point (pH/ORP or conductivity sensor) in a process plant: retract the sensor from the process, clean off fouling, rinse, re-calibrate against buffers and return it to service, documenting the result.

Field corrective maintenance on installed measurement instrumentation on a plant floor or test cell: pressure/temperature transmitters, thermocouples, flow meters, load cells and platform scales - troubleshoot wiring and fittings, replace seals, sensors or a failed transmitter, re-zero and verify, working around live process equipment and other trades.

tasks.label: Conduct calibration tests to determine performance or reliability of mechanical, structural, or electromechanical equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Calibration lab bench work on dimensional gauges that motorized universal length/indicator benches are built for: dial and digital indicators, gauge blocks, plug and ring gauges, calipers, height gauges. Tech pulls the item from the job queue, mounts it, runs the point-by-point comparison against length standards in a temperature-controlled lab, records deviations and pass/fail.

Calibration lab bench work on hand tools requiring manual manipulation and judgment: outside/inside micrometers (thimble and ratchet feel), hardness testers with test blocks, surface plates, spirit levels, thread gauges, and odd legacy mechanical instruments arriving in varied condition needing cleaning and functional checks first.

Lab/workshop calibration of pressure, force, torque and mass instruments: pressure gauges and transmitters on a pressure controller or piston gauge, load cells and force gauges on a deadweight or comparison force machine, torque wrenches and transducers on a torque loader, mass standards on a comparator. Multi-point up/down runs, repeatability, documented results.

Performance and reliability testing of electromechanical/mechanical assemblies on test stands in a manufacturing test area: motors, actuators, gearboxes, transfer cases, valves run through dynamic performance cycles with instrumented fixtures, data acquisition, and accept/reject determination.

On-site calibration at a customer facility (plant, hospital, warehouse): technician brings portable standards and verifies installed or in-service devices in place - process pressure/temperature transmitters, panel gauges, assembly-line torque tools, bench and floor scales - connecting to each device where it sits, running the test points, and issuing a certificate.

Large-scale and outdoor field tests: truck scale/weighbridge calibration with certified test weights and a weight truck, crane and hoist load tests, on-site verification of installed universal testing machines and structural test rigs, tank/silo weighing systems - variable weather, uneven ground, heavy rigging.

instances.label: Receipt/bench inspection in the calibration lab of hand-held dimensional standards and mechanical gauges (gauge blocks, micrometers, calipers, dial indicators, ring/plug gauges): technician picks the item up, tilts it under bench light or magnifier, looks for nicks, burrs, scratches, corrosion, wear on measuring faces, damaged spindles/anvils and illegible scales, and records the condition-on-receipt on the calibration record.

Receipt/bench inspection in the lab of electronic test equipment (DMMs, oscilloscopes, power supplies, signal generators, RF gear, probes and leads): checking case dents and cracks, cracked or burned displays, bent/corroded connector pins, damaged BNC/banana jacks, frayed cords, corroded battery contacts and missing hardware before electrical calibration.

Bench inspection of other lab artifacts and tools: mass standards (scratches, corrosion, adhering dirt), torque wrenches and force gauges, liquid-in-glass and probe thermometers, pipettes and glassware (chips, cracks, clouding), pressure gauges (cracked crystals, bent pointers) — often needing a loupe or a specific lighting angle.

On-site visual inspection during field calibration at a customer plant floor (process plant, factory, hospital biomed shop): walking to installed transmitters, gauges, thermowells, load cells and flow meters, checking for corrosion, cracked gauge glass, leaking/loose fittings, damaged conduit and cabling, and physical damage before and after adjustment.

Field inspection at remote or outdoor unstructured sites (wellhead pads, tank farms, pole/pad-mounted instrumentation, temporary test setups, construction and utility field locations) where layout varies site to site, weather and lighting are uncontrolled, and access to the instrument surfaces is awkward.

tasks.label: Calibrate devices by comparing measurements of pressure, temperature, humidity, or other environmental conditions to known standards.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench calibration of pressure devices (analog gauges, pressure transmitters, switches, digital test gauges) in an accredited or in-house calibration lab: DUT is fitted with adapters onto a comparator/deadweight tester or automated pressure controller, pressure applied at 5-11 setpoints up and down, as-found readings recorded, device trimmed/adjusted if out of tolerance, as-left data and certificate issued.

Bench calibration of temperature devices (PRTs/RTDs, thermocouples, digital thermometers, bimetal/dial thermometers, temperature transmitters, IR thermometers) in a lab using dry-block calibrators, stirred baths, furnaces or blackbody sources against a reference standard and readout; multiple setpoints, stabilization waits, data recorded and certificate/report produced.

Lab calibration of humidity and other environmental-condition instruments (thermo-hygrometers, dew-point meters, RH/T data loggers, chamber sensors) against a two-pressure humidity generator or saturated-salt standards at several %RH/temperature points, with results recorded, adjustment or correction factors applied, and a certificate issued.

On-site calibration of installed process instruments at a customer plant or refinery: locate the transmitter, isolate and vent it, hook up a hand pump/dry block and documenting calibrator, run a multi-point as-found check of the pressure or temperature loop, trim the transmitter, run as-left, restore to service and upload the record.

On-site work at a pharma, biotech or hospital facility calibrating removable environmental monitoring hardware: RH/temperature data loggers, wireless sensors and reference probes are collected, verified against bath/humidity standards on a portable or lab bench, adjusted, and returned for chamber/room mapping and monitoring service.

In-place verification and adjustment of permanently mounted room, cleanroom, freezer or stability-chamber temperature/RH sensors during a site visit: a reference probe is placed next to the installed sensor in the occupied space or chamber, readings compared at ambient/actual conditions, and the controller or transmitter offset adjusted in situ.

In-house/OEM lab, high volume: repeat teardown of one standard model (a fleet of identical gauges, sensors or utility meters recalled on schedule) — same fixture, same fasteners, same internal inspection checklist and reassembly procedure on every unit.

instances.label: Code weld QA in a fabrication shop or pipe/vessel shop: shear-wave, phased array or TOFD ultrasonic examination of butt welds on plate, structural steel, pipe spools or pressure-vessel seams; the piece sits on stands/rollers, the technician couples and manipulates the probe, interprets A-scans, sizes and locates indications and writes an AWS D1.1 / ASME Section V report.

In-service ultrasonic thickness / corrosion mapping on large, accessible steel surfaces at an operating facility: aboveground storage tank floors and shells, vessel walls, stacks, large-bore piping; the plant is running, surfaces are painted or lightly scaled, readings are gridded and reported against API 653/510/570 minimum thicknesses.

In-service ultrasonic work on congested or awkward plant equipment: small-bore piping in racks, insulated lines with inspection ports, elbows, nozzles and boiler tubes reached from scaffold or man-lift, plus shear-wave crack checks on in-service welds; hot surfaces, restricted access, one-off positions.

Production/QC volumetric ultrasonic inspection of manufactured components at a mill or factory: forgings, castings, billets, bar, plate, tube, railway wheels and axles, aerospace laminates; repeated identical parts inspected to a fixed procedure with accept/reject to spec and throughput expectations.

Field ultrasonic inspection of structures and in-service assets at unstructured sites: pipeline girth welds in a right-of-way ditch during construction, bridge members and pins, wind-tower welds, dockside ship hull plating, offshore structural members; weather, mud, access equipment, no fixed layout.

Shop ultrasonic inspection of removed transport components at a maintenance facility: railcar axles and wheels, aircraft wheels and engine disks, shafts and fittings, each part carried to an inspection station or immersion tank and examined to an overhaul specification.

On-vehicle ultrasonic inspection in a hangar or maintenance bay: scanning an assembled aircraft's skin, composite panel or lug after suspected impact/lightning damage, or a weld on an assembled railcar/truck frame, working at height on stands around the machine.

tasks.label: Make radiographic images to detect flaws in objects while leaving objects intact.

instances.label: Field radiography of new-construction welds outdoors — pipeline right-of-way girth welds, plant/structural erection sites. Radiographer hauls a gamma camera or portable X-ray tube (or runs an internal pipe crawler), tapes film/imaging plates around the joint, barricades the radiation area, shoots and processes each weld to code (API 1104/ASME) in mud, wind, heat, at ground level or on scaffold.

Cabinet/vault radiography of production parts in a manufacturing plant — castings, forgings, machined aerospace and additive components, small weldments. Parts are brought to a shielded enclosure or interlocked room, positioned on a table/manipulator between source and digital detector, imaged (2D DR or CT) and evaluated against acceptance criteria in batches.

Shop radiography of large weldments in a fabrication shop bay — pressure-vessel shells, pipe spools, tank and structural welds too big for a cabinet. Radiographer rigs the source (crane, boom, hand placement), tapes imaging plates along the seam, clears and ropes off the bay (often night shift), shoots multiple exposures per joint and reads them.

In-service radiography during a plant turnaround at a refinery, chemical plant or power station — welds and components on congested piping racks, often at height on scaffold, restricted permits, night work, film/CR or portable DR, with exclusion zones set among other trades.

Corrosion/CUI profile radiography of in-service insulated aboveground piping in an operating plant — long runs of insulated line imaged while product flows, capturing pipe wall from several views to map wall loss, access by ladder, lift or rope.

Aerospace/MRO radiography on assembled structures — aircraft in a hangar or engine/airframe assemblies on the floor: shooting fastener rows, bonded joints, composite repairs and honeycomb in situ with a portable source and imaging plate, hangar cleared for the shot.

In-service aboveground storage tank inspection at a terminal or power plant: select and calibrate ultrasonic thickness/corrosion-mapping equipment on step wedges, then scan tank floor and shell to gather API 653 thickness data (tank may be cleaned and opened, or inspected on-stream).

Field survey of in-service plant equipment at a refinery, chemical plant or power station: UT thickness readings at condition monitoring locations on piping and vessels, boiler-tube corrosion mapping, and eddy-current/IRIS heat-exchanger tube inspection during a turnaround; gear carried to scaffolds, ladders and confined spaces, calibrated on-site with reference blocks, insulation and coatings variable.

MRO hangar or component overhaul shop (aircraft, rail, heavy vehicle): eddy-current, ultrasonic, penetrant or X-ray inspection of removed components (wheels, blades, shafts, brackets) and of installed structure, with instruments standardized on reference specimens before each inspection lot.

Civil infrastructure assessment: bridge deck or concrete structure survey with GPR, impact echo, ultrasonic surface waves, half-cell/electrical resistivity equipment; equipment calibrated/verified on-site, data collected over a deck under lane closure in traffic and weather.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Fabrication shop / manufacturing plant: visual examination (VT) of welds, castings, forgings and machined components for cracks, porosity, undercut, laps, and surface corrosion under controlled lighting, using magnifiers, mirrors and weld gauges; indications recorded against AWS/ASME acceptance criteria, often as the precursor to UT/PT/MT.

Internal remote visual inspection of assembled machinery and vessels with borescopes, videoscopes, fiber optics and push cameras: aero-engine blades and combustors on-wing or in the engine shop, gas/steam turbine internals, gearboxes, heat-exchanger tubes, pump and valve bodies. The inspector threads a probe through small access ports, articulates the tip, and calls indications against manual limits.

In-service aboveground storage tank at a fuel terminal or refinery: internal examination of the floor and shell for corrosion, pitting and coating breakdown, producing an API 653-type condition report without confined-space entry where possible.

Aircraft exterior structural visual inspection in an MRO hangar: full fuselage, wing and empennage skin survey for lightning-strike burns, dents, corrosion, cracked skins and paint damage; findings mapped, sized and reported against the maintenance manual.

Remote camera inspection of hard-to-access field assets: buried sewer/culvert pipe runs surveyed by CCTV crawler launched from manholes, and wind turbine blades/towers surveyed for cracks, erosion, delamination and lightning damage; deliverable is a coded/annotated defect report.

Field close visual inspection of civil and industrial structures taken as found: bridge girders and welds, tank and vessel exteriors, structural steel, offshore and plant piping; access by lift, scaffold or rope, surfaces wire-brushed by hand, cracks sized with gauges, weather and lighting variable.

instances.label: Aboveground storage tank at a refinery, terminal or tank farm: internal floor and shell corrosion survey with ultrasonic thickness mapping, delivered as an API 653-style condition report. Normally requires emptying, cleaning and confined-space entry; large plate steel surfaces, product residues, poor lighting.

In-situ weld and pressure-equipment examination during a plant turnaround or at a fabrication/construction site (refinery, power or nuclear plant, chemical plant): radiography and phased-array ultrasonics of piping welds, vessel seams and boiler tubes, plus MT/PT. Access by scaffold, rope or man-lift; insulation removal, hot surfaces, confined spaces, congested pipe racks.

Aircraft in an MRO hangar or on a maintenance ramp: exterior condition examination after lightning strike, hail or bird strike, and scheduled general visual inspection of skin, lap joints and control surfaces, documented to maintenance-manual requirements for return to service.

Manufactured or overhauled components presented at an inspection station in a factory or repair shop: composite wing/fuselage panels, castings, forgings, welded assemblies, wheels and axles examined by ultrasonic, eddy-current or radiographic methods against written acceptance criteria.

Transmission pipeline segment: full-length internal examination between launcher and receiver for metal loss, cracking and deformation while the line stays in service, delivered as a located and sized anomaly list for integrity management.

Bridge, dam, penstock or tower in the field: routine condition survey and documentation of the structure over water or live traffic, covering under-deck, pier, girder and high-elevation surfaces that otherwise need snooper trucks, rope access or lane closures.

tasks.label: Produce images of objects on film, using radiographic techniques.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Pipeline construction right-of-way: radiograph girth welds on new transmission pipe. Technician wraps film (or an imaging plate) and IQIs around the outside of the joint, sets the barricade/radiation boundary, runs an Ir-192 projector or sends an internal crawler source to the weld, exposes, then processes film in a mobile darkroom. Weather, mud, sloped ROW, dozens of joints per shift.

Refinery, chemical plant or power-plant turnaround: radiograph new or repair welds in process piping, headers and vessel nozzles. Welds at elevation on scaffold or in congested pipe racks, often on night shift with the area cordoned; source cranked out on a guide tube, film taped to the opposite wall of the pipe, multiple shots per weld, film processed in a shack.

Fabrication / pipe-spool / structural shop radiography bay: weldments, spools, valves and castings staged on carts or benches inside a shielded room. Technician selects the technique (kV, SFD, time), lays out film cassettes, lead letters and IQIs, makes the exposures, and processes the film to a required density and sensitivity.

Serial production radiography at a foundry or aerospace plant: the same part type (aluminum castings, wheels, turbine blades, weldments) presented repeatedly to a cabinet/vault X-ray line on a conveyor, cart or turntable, with a fixed, qualified technique and 100% or sampling coverage.

Operating plant / tank farm: profile (tangential) radiographic imaging along runs of in-service insulated or bare piping to image wall loss and corrosion under insulation, with the line still in service; access at grade, on scaffold or by rope, with a controlled radiation boundary.

tasks.label: Conduct liquid penetrant tests to locate surface cracks by coating objects with fluorescent dyes, cleaning excess penetrant, and applying developer.

instances.label: Batch fluorescent penetrant inspection of aerospace/turbine hardware (blades, vanes, discs, castings, machined details) in a plant or MRO NDT department: parts racked in baskets/fixtures and taken through pre-clean, penetrant application, dwell, emulsifier, rinse, dry, developer, then examined in a darkened UV booth and dispositioned.

Bench/small-unit penetrant testing of individual transportable parts (foundry castings, machined components, tooling, welded coupons) at a job-shop or lab darkroom: aerosol or small dip application of fluorescent penetrant, solvent/water removal of excess, developer, UV examination, mark and report indications.

In-place penetrant testing on large fabrications or installed machinery inside a fab shop or plant (weld seams on frames and vessels, repair welds, casting rework areas): the part is not moved, so the tech works from a ladder or the floor with aerosol penetrant, solvent-dampened rags, aerosol developer and a portable UV lamp under a shroud.

Field penetrant testing at industrial/construction sites: pipeline girth welds, structural steel connections, refinery piping and vessel welds during turnaround, often outdoors on scaffolds or in a ditch, variable weather, surface prep by grinding/solvent, portable kit, darkened enclosure needed for the fluorescent method.

In-situ penetrant testing on installed equipment inside an institution-controlled facility: aircraft structure/landing gear fittings in a maintenance hangar, turbine casings, crane hooks, valve bodies in a power plant — confined and awkward access, work performed around the assembly with portable materials and UV lamp.

instances.label: Weld flaw detection and mapping in fabrication shops and operating plants: shear-wave/phased-array/TOFD scanning of girth and seam welds on piping, pressure vessels and structural steel; inspector calibrates on a reference block, couples and hand-scans crown-to-crown, and plots indication position, length and through-wall depth on a weld map for code acceptance.

Corrosion/erosion thickness mapping of large accessible surfaces of in-service equipment at a plant or fuel terminal: storage tank floors and shell courses, boiler waterwall tubing, large vessel walls; dense grid or C-scan readings converted into a wall-loss map for API 653/510 fitness-for-service.

Thickness/corrosion mapping on piping and complex geometry inside a plant: small-bore lines, elbows, tees, nozzles, insulated lines with inspection ports, often on scaffold, ladders or in confined spaces, producing a gridded remaining-wall map.

Production NDT of manufactured parts in a factory inspection department: composite aerostructures, forgings, castings, plate, billet, engine disks and blades; immersion, squirter or contact ultrasonic scanning producing a C-scan map of porosity, delamination or inclusions against accept/reject criteria.

In-service inspection of transportation assets in maintenance facilities: on-aircraft composite skin and metallic structure scanned in a hangar for disbonds and cracks, and rail wheels, axles and vehicle components in a depot or overhaul shop, with the indication extent mapped.

Field inspection at unstructured sites: bridge members and pins, offshore/marine structures, pipeline dig sites, remote wellheads and construction sites; access by rope, man-lift or excavation, variable weather and surface condition, no fixed layout.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Route-based thermographic (IR) inspection round inside a power plant, refinery, or factory: capture radiometric images at defined inspection points on accessible assets (motors, pumps, bearings, steam/process piping, transformers, panels with IR windows), trend temperatures, flag and report anomalies for maintenance.

Thermographic survey of large outdoor industrial assets from the air or a remote platform: solar arrays, utility substations and transformers, tank roofs, flare/stack equipment; capture thermal imagery over the whole asset, analyze for hot/cold anomalies, issue O&M report.

Acoustic emission testing of in-service pressure equipment (vessels, storage tanks, piping, spheres) at a plant: mount and couple AE sensor arrays with magnetic hold-downs/couplant, verify coupling by pencil-lead break, monitor during controlled pressurization, locate and grade emission sources per code, plus close-access contact/IR work on insulation and refractory reached by ladder or scaffold.

Leak testing of manufactured components and assemblies in a fabrication shop or QC area: helium sniffer or vacuum-chamber mass spectrometer testing, pressure/vacuum decay, bubble testing of welds and seals on repeat production parts, with pass/fail records.

Field leak detection survey on installed pressurized systems at an operating facility: acoustic/ultrasonic imaging for compressed air, steam and vacuum leaks, gas sniffing/tracer-gas surveys on piping, valves and flanges; locate, quantify and report losses.

Developing or qualifying a new/adapted technique: designing the setup on seeded-flaw reference specimens in a lab, running trials to establish detectability and parameters, then writing and validating the written procedure against code and customer requirements.

tasks.label: Identify defects in concrete or other building materials, using thermal or infrared testing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-service concrete bridge deck or elevated parking deck delamination survey: work zone with lane closures on a public structure, IR imaging (handheld, vehicle- or drone-mounted) during the solar-loading window, variable weather and traffic, findings correlated with visual survey and hammer/chain sounding, deliverable is a quantified delamination map.

Exterior facade/wall thermographic survey of an existing occupied building (brick, tile cladding, precast concrete panels, EIFS) for debonding, voids and moisture; access from ground, boom lift, swing stage or drone; building and surroundings taken as found.

Low-slope commercial roof and roof-deck moisture survey, usually after sunset: walk-over IR or aerial thermal scan to map wet insulation and deteriorated deck, mark areas on the roof, produce moisture map and report; roof cluttered with penetrations, equipment, ponding and debris.

Concrete structures inside an owner-controlled facility: parking garage, water/wastewater plant, power plant, tunnel, industrial building. Scheduled scans of walls, slabs, columns and linings for delamination, voids, moisture ingress or refractory/insulation loss during maintenance rounds or outages.

Precast plant, fabrication shop or NDT lab: active (heat-applied) thermography on manufactured concrete panels, FRP-strengthened elements, bonded repairs and specimens under controlled indoor conditions, producing QC accept/reject decisions and documentation.

Active construction or rehabilitation site QA: thermal testing of new concrete placements, FRP wrap bond, grouted tendon ducts or repair mortars amid ongoing trades, moving scaffolding, temporary power and changing weather.

instances.label: Aerospace/metals QC shop or lab: eddy-current electrical conductivity (%IACS) measurement on aluminum plate, extrusions, forgings and machined parts to verify heat-treat condition, sort alloys, or assess heat/fire damage. Worker calibrates the meter on conductivity standards, places the probe on clean flat areas at several locations, and compares readings to the specification.

Hangar/plant: conductivity and other electrical readings taken on assembled or in-service hardware (aircraft skins and fittings, weldments, castings in place). Curved surfaces, coatings, fasteners and restricted access; several point readings mapped over an area and judged against acceptance limits.

QC/materials laboratory: rheometric flow measurement of process fluids and materials — penetrant and emulsifier baths, couplants, oils/greases, resins or polymer melt. Sample is poured or loaded into a rotational rheometer/viscometer or melt-flow tester, run at controlled temperature and shear, result compared to spec, logged, and the instrument cleaned.

Field survey of reinforced concrete (bridge deck, parking garage, marine or industrial structure): half-cell potential and four-electrode (Wenner) resistivity readings on a marked grid, with a connection to the rebar mat, over dirty/wet surfaces under traffic control and weather; results mapped to evaluate concrete quality and corrosion severity.

Electrical output and continuity verification in shops and at job sites: measuring magnetizing amperage on magnetic-particle benches per ASTM E1444, verifying x-ray tube kV/mA, bonding/continuity and insulation-resistance checks on structures and wiring, cathodic-protection test-station potentials, and occasional RF/radiometric checks — hooking meters, shunts and clamps to terminals and test points.

tasks.label: Maintain clean working environments, according to clean room standards.

instances.label: End-of-job upkeep of the technician's own workstation in a photonics lab or cleanroom: wiping the optical table, breadboard and equipment housings with IPA and lint-free wipes, blowing/removing dust and debris around mounted optics, cables and fixtures, and returning tools and components to their storage, all amid delicate aligned setups that must not be disturbed.

Scheduled floor care in the lab and cleanroom gray space: HEPA vacuuming, mopping or scrubbing open floor areas and aisles on a fixed route, on an institution-controlled and predictable layout, during off-shift or low-traffic hours.

SOP-driven cleaning of the room fabric to cleanroom standards: wiping walls, windows, pass-through chambers, gowning benches, chairs, and laminar-flow hood/enclosure interiors with cleanroom wipes and prescribed solvents using unidirectional overlapping strokes, and changing tacky mats.

Waste handling: emptying receptacles of used wipes, gloves and packaging, segregating and containing solvent- or epoxy-contaminated waste, replacing liners, and hauling waste containers out through the gowning corridor or airlock to the waste area.

Consumables and gowning-area upkeep: restocking gloves, wipes, booties, mop heads and solvent bottles, wiping down tools, carts and packaged items as they are passed into the cleanroom through the airlock, and keeping the gowning room and supply shelves orderly.

Cleanliness verification rounds: taking airborne particle counts at defined monitoring points on a schedule, checking pressure differentials and surface cleanliness, recording results and flagging excursions for corrective action.

tasks.label: Adjust or maintain equipment, such as lasers, laser systems, microscopes, oscilloscopes, pulse generators, power meters, beam analyzers, or energy measurement devices.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench alignment/adjustment of a laser or free-space optical system during build, test, or troubleshooting in the employer's photonics lab or test bay: peaking output power, walking a resonator or beam-delivery mirror pair, adjusting kinematic mounts and translation stages by hand while watching a power meter or beam profiler, coupling a beam into a fiber, then documenting the result.

Alignment and coupling of photonic devices on a production/test line: active alignment of fiber arrays or lens elements to laser diodes or photonic chips, pigtailing, sub-micron positioning, and locking/attaching the aligned part, on a manufacturer's floor with standard fixtures and repeat part types.

Setting up, adjusting, zeroing and calibrating/verifying measurement equipment: connecting detector heads, probes and cables to power meters, energy meters, beam analyzers, oscilloscopes and pulse generators; positioning detectors in the beam; configuring ranges/triggers; running a calibration or verification against a reference and applying adjustments.

Routine upkeep of an enclosed industrial laser system (cutting/welding/marking machine) on a shop floor: inspecting and replacing the cutting nozzle and protective cover glass, checking filters, gas and beam-path condition, monitoring process parameters, and running a test cut/power check.

Component-level maintenance and repair of lasers, microscopes and optical instruments: opening a laser head or instrument, cleaning or replacing contaminated/damaged optics, swapping flashlamps, diode modules, lamps or filters, servicing chillers and purge lines, reassembling, then realigning and verifying performance; failure mode and unit condition vary case to case.

On-site adjustment and service of installed photonic equipment away from the home facility: an industrial laser at a customer plant, a clinical/medical laser, telecom fiber plant gear, or a field-deployed lidar/rangefinder — access is cramped and layouts, mounting and ambient conditions differ at every site.

tasks.label: Assist scientists or engineers in the conduct of photonic experiments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: University/corporate optics lab: technician sets up a free-space optical experiment per the scientist's sketch — mounts mirrors, lenses, beamsplitters, polarizers and detectors on a breadboard, routes the beam, aligns it through the chain, couples into a fiber or spectrometer, and verifies beam quality before handing the setup over.

Research lab: technician runs the experiment alongside the scientist — powers and sets the laser, sweeps parameters, operates spectrometer/power meter/camera, watches for thermal drift and re-peaks alignment mid-run, and logs the data set the scientist needs.

Lab bench: technician mounts and swaps the items under study — sample cells, photonic chips, filters, gratings — and prepares fiber (strip, cleave, splice, connectorize, polish), then re-establishes coupling for each new device.

Lab and shop: technician builds and installs the supporting hardware for an experiment — machines or assembles one-off brackets and enclosures, bolts instruments into racks, runs power/signal cables and fiber between benches, installs a newly delivered laser or stage, and occasionally relocates a setup to another room or test site.

Research lab: technician troubleshoots and maintains the experiment when it fails — traces why the signal vanished, checks connectors and drivers, replaces a dead diode/detector/controller board, services and re-certifies the laser, cleans contaminated optics, and performs interlock/safety checks.

Cleanroom or fab test bay: technician supports engineers characterizing photonic integrated circuits — loads wafers or singulated die, couples fiber arrays or probes to grating couplers/facets, runs wafer- or die-level optical and opto-electronic test sequences, and returns the measurement data.

tasks.label: Test or perform failure analysis for optomechanical or optoelectrical products, according to test plans.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production functional test of packaged optoelectronic devices (laser diodes, VCSEL modules, transceivers, detector assemblies) at a test station on a manufacturing floor or cleanroom: load DUT into socket/fixture, mate fiber, run LIV/spectral/BER sequence per the test plan, log data, pass/fail bin.

Die-, wafer- or chip-level optical/electro-optical characterization of photonic components (PICs, VCSELs, gratings, modulators) on a probe station or optical bench in an engineering lab: align optical coupling, probe electrically, sweep wavelength/current, record spectra and responsivity per the test plan.

Reliability and environmental qualification: mount units in burn-in racks, thermal chambers or on vibration fixtures, connect drive/monitor lines and fibers, run stress per the qual plan over hours-to-weeks, take periodic optical power/spectral readings and flag degradation.

Bench-level test of assembled optomechanical products (lens/camera modules, laser heads, optical instruments): fixture the assembly, verify alignment, run interferometric wavefront, MTF/EFL or beam-profile measurements against the test plan, record results.

Production failure triage of units that failed the line test: retest the failing unit on the automated station, isolate which parameter/channel is out of spec, re-bin or route to rework, log failure mode.

In-depth failure analysis of a returned or field-failed optomechanical/optoelectronic product in an FA lab: partial disassembly, microscope and emission/thermal inspection, electrical probing, cross-section or decap as needed, iterative hypothesis testing, root-cause report.

On-site test of installed optical/fiber systems at a customer site, telecom outside plant, or an integrated laser system in a varied facility: locate and clean/inspect connectors, run OTDR/insertion-loss or power/alignment checks per the test plan, work around whatever layout and access is found.

instances.label: Photonics R&D lab bench: technician splices a specialty fiber (PM, large-mode-area, or dissimilar-cladding fiber) into a laser or test setup — strips coating, cleans, cleaves, aligns (including rotational alignment for PM), fuses, recoats or sleeves, proof-tests and measures splice loss. Indoor lab, controlled temperature/cleanliness, benchtop splicer or glass processor at hand.

Optical component / fiber-laser production floor: repeated pigtail and combiner splices on assemblies (e.g., pump combiner leads, delivery fibers, pigtailing a module), dozens per shift at a dedicated splicing workstation in a controlled production area or cleanroom, with fixed recipes and documented loss/tension records.

Installation or repair inside a customer facility (data center, telecom central office, campus riser, hospital equipment room): splicing pigtails onto cable fibers inside rack-mounted splice trays or wall enclosures; cramped access, work performed at the enclosure on a ladder or in a rack aisle, live equipment nearby, verify with OTDR/power meter.

Outside-plant field splice: splice closure in a manhole, pedestal, aerial bucket or splice trailer; open/prepare cable sheath, route buffer tubes, make dozens to hundreds of single or mass-ribbon splices, seat them in trays, seal the closure; dirt, wind, temperature, poor lighting, cramped posture.

Emergency field service on installed equipment at a customer site: repairing a broken delivery fiber or sensor lead inside or next to a machine (fiber laser head, medical/industrial system) — access is awkward and site-specific, splice must be made, protected and verified in situ with the equipment partly disassembled.

tasks.label: Build prototype optomechanical devices for use in equipment such as aerial cameras, gun sights, or telescopes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In the company optics lab/clean assembly area, build a prototype free-space optical subassembly on a baseplate or breadboard: place and secure mirrors, lenses, beamsplitters, filters in mounts per the engineer's layout, align beam path with autocollimator/laser and detector feedback, lock down and verify.

Build a prototype lens cell/barrel assembly: clean and install multiple elements with spacers into machined cells, secure with retaining rings or structural adhesive, then verify centration/wavefront on a centration tester or interferometer and rework if out of spec.

Actively align and bond an optical assembly to a detector or emitter for a prototype aerial camera or sight head (lens assembly to focal-plane array, reticle projector or laser diode to collimator), using UV/structural epoxy with live image or power feedback, then verify focus/MTF/boresight.

Mechanical build-up of the prototype housing: fit brackets and shims, drill/tap/deburr or file one-off machined parts to make them fit, torque fasteners, route and dress cables, mate connectors, install seals/desiccant and close the housing.

Iterative prototype rework and troubleshooting under engineering direction: disassemble a failing build, diagnose the cause (pinched wire, stressed optic, wrong shim, contamination), re-clean optics, adjust or remake a part, reassemble and re-test.

Final integration of the optical head into the system-level prototype (gimbal, gun-sight body, telescope tube) in the integration lab, plus boresighting and functional/environmental checkout per the test plan.

tasks.label: Terminate, cure, polish, or test fiber cables with mechanical connectors.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Photonics lab / prototype shop bench: technician makes a handful of custom patch cords or pigtails with standard epoxy-and-polish connectors (FC, SC, LC, ST) on standard single-mode or multimode fiber — strip and clean, inject epoxy, insert fiber, oven-cure, scribe, hand/machine polish through film steps, clean, scope the end face and run IL/RL. Mixed connector types, small batch sizes, human-height bench with ovens, pucks and a polishing machine.

Production or pilot-line assembly area of a photonics/fiber-assembly manufacturer: repetitive termination of standard LC/SC/MPO connectors in volume on cut-to-length cable, using epoxy dispensers, curing ovens, multi-position production polishing machines with quick-change fixtures, automated end-face interferometry and multichannel IL/RL test racks; documented per-part results.

Specialty or exotic terminations at the bench: polarization-maintaining fiber keyed to the connector, large-core / high-power laser delivery fiber, fiber bundles, custom or non-standard ferrules and metal connectors, angled or specialty polishes; one-off or few-off jobs where the recipe is developed as the technician goes and acceptance is by interferometer plus optical performance test.

In-situ termination with field-installable mechanical connectors (cam/crimp splice-type or splice-on) on cable already pulled into a lab, cleanroom or equipment room: cable end reached in a patch panel, tray or enclosure, strip, cleave, insert, crimp, dress the fiber into the tray, then verify with visual fault locator, power meter or OTDR.

Bench inspection, test and rework of already-terminated assemblies: scope and clean end faces, run insertion-loss/return-loss and OTDR checks, re-polish or re-terminate rejects, record results against Telcordia/IEC acceptance criteria.

Customer site or outdoor installation: terminating and testing fiber at a rack, enclosure or instrument in a building under construction, a shipboard/vehicle installation, or an outdoor test range; variable lighting, cramped access, portable kit only.

tasks.label: Perform diagnostic analyses of processing steps, using analytical or metrological tools, such as microscopy, profilometry, or ellipsometry devices.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume semiconductor / photonic-IC fab: after a deposition, etch or litho step, production wafers are measured on inline metrology and inspection tools (spectroscopic ellipsometry/reflectometry for film thickness, OCD, patterned-wafer defect inspection). Wafers arrive in FOUPs at SEMI load ports; the technician sets up/monitors recipes, reviews automatically generated charts, and flags out-of-spec lots.

Mid-size or research cleanroom (university nanofab, PIC/MEMS/thin-film shop): technician carries a wafer or diced coupon from the process tool to a shared standalone ellipsometer, stylus/optical profilometer or inspection microscope, mounts it by hand, picks measurement sites, fits thickness/step height, and logs whether the process step met target.

Optics/coating production area: polished or coated lenses, prisms, mirrors and witness samples checked after grinding, polishing or coating - cosmetic scratch/dig inspection under microscope per ISO 10110-7/MIL, surface figure on an interferometer, roughness or coating step height on a profilometer - with pass/fail and a measurement report per lot.

Fiber-optic connector/ferrule assembly workshop: after epoxy cure and polishing, endface geometry (radius, apex offset, fiber height) is measured on an interferometer and endface cleanliness/scratches graded per IEC 61300-3-35 under a video microscope; failures are sent back for re-polish and the polishing process is adjusted.

R&D / pilot-line lab: routine characterization of a batch of development samples on standard substrates - film thickness maps by ellipsometry, coating defect imaging, profilometry of patterned features - repeated across a designed process split and fed back to the engineer as a trend.

Open-ended process troubleshooting: an unfamiliar or oddly shaped sample (prototype waveguide chip, failed bonded assembly, unknown multilayer stack); the technician decides which technique to apply, improvises mounting/alignment, builds or adapts an optical model, cross-correlates microscope, profilometer and ellipsometer results, and diagnoses the offending process step.

tasks.label: Assemble or adjust parts or related electrical units of prototypes to prepare for testing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Free-space optical prototype built on a breadboard/optical table in an R&D photonics lab: technician mounts laser source, lenses, mirrors, beamsplitters, polarizers and detectors on posts and kinematic mounts, sets the beam path and brings it to coarse/fine alignment so the setup can be tested (interferometer, beam-shaping, imaging or laser-cavity prototype).

Photonic module/package prototype in a cleanroom or assembly lab: technician actively aligns and attaches a fiber array, micro-lens, laser diode or PIC chiplet to a submount/bench with sub-micron accuracy while monitoring coupled optical power, then fixes it with UV epoxy, solder or laser weld before the module goes to test.

Electrical subassembly for the prototype at an ESD bench: populate or rework a small driver/control PCB, solder wire leads, pigtails, thermistor and TEC leads, connector solder cups and headers, so the electrical unit is ready to be powered and tested.

System integration of a one-off prototype into a chassis or enclosure: bolt optomechanical mounts, laser head, TEC/heatsink and boards into the housing, route and dress cables and fiber, crimp/plug connectors to drivers, controllers and power supplies, and tie the wiring off for test.

Adjustment/tuning of an existing prototype after a test result: re-peak beam alignment or fiber-coupling efficiency, tweak mirror/lens tip-tilt and translation stages, reposition an optic, and re-verify with a power meter or camera before the next test run.

tasks.label: Repair or calibrate products, such as surgical lasers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-house final alignment and calibration of a finished laser/optical product on the manufacturer's production or test bench: align resonator or beam-delivery optics, couple the output, measure power, beam profile and wavelength, trim to spec, log results.

Depot/bench repair of a returned or failed unit (e.g., a surgical laser with low output or an error code): diagnose from symptoms and test data, open the enclosure, isolate the failed subassembly (flashlamp, diode module, power board, contaminated optic), replace it, reassemble, realign and retest.

On-site preventive maintenance and calibration of a surgical/medical laser in a hospital OR, surgery center or biomed shop: verify output at the fiber tip against spec with a power meter, check aiming beam, footswitch and interlocks, replace worn fiber/handpiece, adjust calibration, complete service documentation.

On-site service of an industrial or scientific laser system at a customer plant or lab: realign the beam delivery path, replace a contaminated protective window/lens/mirror, verify focus, power and beam quality, troubleshoot chiller/electronics faults in a machine as found.

Routine consumable and beam-path maintenance check on an enclosed industrial laser machine tool: change/clean the cutting nozzle and verify nozzle condition and beam centering before production resumes.

Calibration/verification of optical test instruments and detectors (laser power/energy meters, spectrometers, beam profilers) against traceable standards in the calibration lab, with adjustment and issuance of a calibration record.

Repair/rework of fiber-optic assemblies and photonic modules on the bench: re-terminate or splice a pigtail, clean and inspect connectors, re-couple the fiber to the emitter, verify insertion loss/coupled power.

tasks.label: Design, build, or modify fixtures used to assemble parts.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Ad-hoc bench fixture in an optics lab or on a production bench: technician must hold a lens barrel, laser sub-assembly or fiber pigtail steady for epoxy bonding/alignment; selects posts, clamps, V-blocks, magnetic bases, brackets and tooling plates from stock, bolts them to a breadboard, test-fits the actual part and re-works the arrangement until it constrains the part repeatably and leaves the work accessible.

Designs a new custom fixture: measures the part with calipers/gauges, models the nest and clamping scheme in CAD, picks material, clearances and tolerances, produces a drawing or print file, then checks the first article against real parts and revises the design.

Fabricates a fixture to an existing drawing/model in the in-house shop or print room: cuts and mills an aluminum base plate, drills and taps mounting holes, or 3D prints a nest; deburrs, cleans and dimension-checks the finished piece before release.

Diagnoses and modifies an in-service fixture on the assembly floor: nest worn, parts scratching, locator drifted, or a new part revision does not seat; the technician disassembles it, shims, re-drills, adds or repositions clamps/locating pins, then re-qualifies it with sample parts.

Builds a precision micro-fixture in a cleanroom for fiber/laser-diode assembly: bonds or dowel-pins a hardened nest to a base plate to micron tolerances, verifies position under microscope/CMM, and validates with pilot parts before it goes into production.

Optical backplane / fiber shuffle build on a manufacturing floor: routing and adhering multi-fiber ribbons on a flex substrate or backplane frame per a routing map, terminating MT/MPO ferrules, epoxy cure and polish, endface inspection and insertion-loss/return-loss test of every port.

System/rack-level integration on a lab or telecom integration floor: mounting the optical backplane and switch/line cards into a chassis or rack, fastening hardware, routing and dressing fiber harnesses through cable management, cleaning and inspecting endfaces, mating MPO/LC connectors and blind-mate interfaces, powering up and verifying links.

R&D prototype build on an optical table: one-off assembly of a novel optoelectronic interface or photonic-switch demonstrator — mounting collimators, lenses, mirrors, isolators and detectors in adjustable mounts, coupling free-space beams into fiber, iterating alignment and re-fixturing as the design changes.

tasks.label: Mix, pour, or use processing chemicals or gases according to safety standards or established operating procedures.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cleanroom wet-process bench in a photonics/semiconductor fab or university nanofab: technician mixes and pours developer, buffered oxide etch, piranha or solvent baths per SOP, immerses wafers/optical substrates on a timed schedule, cascade-rinses, N2-dries, and decants spent chemistry into labeled waste, gowned and working at a fume-exhausted wet bench.

Optics and fiber cleaning/surface prep in an optics production area or laser lab: mixing detergent and solvent cleaning baths, running ultrasonic/spray cleaning of lenses and mirrors before coating or bonding, and drag-wiping optics and connector end faces with acetone/methanol/IPA per procedure.

Optical and fiber assembly bench: measuring and mixing two-part epoxies, potting compounds and index-matching gels, injecting epoxy into connector ferrules or bonding lenses into mounts within pot-life, oven curing, and solvent cleanup of excess adhesive.

Process gases: exchanging and connecting cylinders and regulators, leak-checking fittings, purging lines with nitrogen, refilling gas-laser gas mixes (CO2, excimer premix), and setting purge/process gas flows at deposition, etch or fiber-draw tooling according to written safety procedures.

General bench chemistry in a fume hood at a photonics R&D or production lab: weighing and dissolving reagents, diluting acids/solvents to a specified concentration per written protocol, mixing and labeling stock solutions, and transferring residues into hazardous-waste carboys.

Field or customer-site work: mixing epoxy for connector termination, using cleaning solvents/gel and dry-gas purges on installed fiber and optics in a telecom hut, rooftop cabinet or customer plant taken as found, with no dedicated chemical station.

tasks.label: Fabricate devices, such as optoelectronic or semiconductor devices.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Wafer-level fabrication in a production semiconductor/photonics fab cleanroom: loading wafer carriers, running lithography, deposition, etch, anneal and dicing recipes on qualified tool sets with in-line metrology, in a gowned, access-controlled cleanroom on standard wafer sizes.

Chip-level packaging on a laser/LED/transceiver production line: die attach of laser diodes, photodiodes, VCSELs or PICs onto submounts and carriers (eutectic or epoxy), wire bonding, dispensing, hermetic/lid seal, at micron placement tolerances and production throughput; parts arrive in waffle packs, trays or on wafer film.

Micro-optical / optomechanical subassembly of a device: placing and actively aligning collimating lenses, mirrors, isolators and filters into a module housing or on a bench, UV-epoxy or laser-weld bonding while monitoring the optical signal, then verifying beam quality/coupling before handoff.

Fiber-based device fabrication: pigtailing output fiber or a fiber array unit to a laser diode or photonic chip, active alignment and bonding, fusion splicing, connector termination and polish, building the finished fiber module.

Prototype / low-volume custom photonic module build in an R&D lab or pilot line: a handful of units to a new drawing, using standard chips, micro-optics and fibers but a new geometry and traveler each time.

Novel device and process development in a shared research nanofab: hand-processing small wafer coupons or odd-shaped samples, improvised fixtures and jigs, tweaking a process flow that does not yet exist, with frequent judgment calls and rework.

roles.description: Perform surveying and mapping duties, usually under the direction of an engineer, surveyor, cartographer, or photogrammetrist, to obtain data used for construction, mapmaking, boundary location, mining, or other purposes. May calculate mapmaking information and create maps from source data, such as surveying notes, aerial photography, satellite data, or other maps to show topographical features, political boundaries, and other features. May verify accuracy and completeness of maps.

tasks.label: Set out and recover stakes, marks, or other monumentation.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Construction grade/offset/slope staking on an active earthwork or roadway job: hauling bundles of lath and hubs across graded dirt, driving hubs and lath at computed station/offset positions, writing station, offset, cut/fill and slope data on each lath in keel, replacing stakes destroyed by equipment, working around moving dozers, mud, brush and traffic control.

Large-site coordinate point layout where a painted ground mark (sometimes with a flag or whisker) is the accepted deliverable: thousands of solar pile locations, foundation/pier grids, road pre-marking for striping, parking-lot layout, marked from a CSV of design coordinates on open graded terrain.

Interior building layout on a concrete slab in a structure under construction: transferring control points and snapping/printing wall lines, door and penetration locations and anchor points onto the floor for the following trades, amid stacked material, other trades and partially built work.

Boundary corner monumentation on private property: setting 5/8" rebar with capped identification, iron pipes, or PK nails/discs in pavement at computed property corners in yards, fence lines, brush and wooded parcels; driving rebar by sledge, avoiding utilities, then flagging and witnessing the monument.

Recovery of existing monumentation: searching a described area with a magnetic locator or metal detector for section corners, old irons, pipes, or benchmark discs; digging through sod, gravel, asphalt shoulder or brush, exposing and cleaning the monument, reading the cap stamping, verifying it against the record and documenting/photographing it.

Setting and recovering permanent survey control and benchmarks: drilling into concrete, curb or bedrock and epoxying a brass/aluminum disc or setting a rebar-and-cap control monument, stamping it, setting hubs, nails and photogrammetric targets along corridors and around a site, and later re-occupying/recovering those marks.

tasks.label: Search for section corners, property irons, or survey points.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Suburban/urban residential boundary retracement: technician works from a deed/plat and prior survey ties to hunt 5/8" rebar, iron pipes or capped pins at lot corners in private yards — sweeping a magnetic locator over lawns, mulch beds, fence lines and driveway edges, probing, then digging a small hole with a shovel to expose the iron, brushing it clean, reading any cap stamping, and deciding whether it is the called-for corner or a stray nail/fence wire.

Rural section, quarter or aliquot corner recovery: driving to a county road intersection or fence corner, interpreting a written monument record ('iron pipe 0.3' below grade, 25' east of power pole'), searching brush, tall grass, ditches and plowed fields with a Schonstedt locator, digging up to a foot or more to expose a stone, pipe or brass cap, and verifying the stamping; mud, snow, ticks, uneven ground, livestock.

Urban street / public right-of-way monument search: locating brass disks in concrete, PK nails, chiseled marks, and monuments inside cast-iron monument boxes in pavement; lifting or prying the lid, cleaning out asphalt, gravel and water to expose the mark, working amid live traffic with cones and a vest.

Active construction or land-development site: searching for previously set control points, hubs, offset stakes, rebar with caps and boundary monuments amid grading, stockpiles, trenching, equipment traffic and disturbed ground; determining which points survived and re-finding buried/partially destroyed ones.

Controlled-access institutional or industrial premises (university campus, airport airside, port terminal, refinery, utility substation, dam): escorted recovery of established survey control marks — brass disks set in concrete pads, floor or wall marks, NGS bench marks — in an area with fixed layout, mown grass or paved surfaces, and an operator controlling access.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous detection/mapping of buried ferrous objects in unstructured outdoor terrain, the sensing half of a monument search. It does not transfer to the whole task: targets were 0.1 m cartridges laid level with the surface, and the system performs no probing, digging, cap-reading, or record-based verification of which monument was found.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous buried-metal geophysical survey on open ground, comparable sensing to a magnetic-locator sweep. It does not cover the survey technician's work of excavating, exposing, cleaning and identifying a particular monument and matching it to record evidence.

instances.label: Open-site layout/stakeout on large graded ground: utility-scale solar pile grids, building pads, trench and ground-improvement grids, road pre-marking. Technician runs GNSS rover/data collector from a network RTK or base station, marks thousands of design coordinates with paint, nails/whiskers or hubs, and records elevations. Flat, cleared, few obstructions.

Detailed construction staking and building layout: sets up total station over control on an active earthwork, utility, road or subdivision job (or on a concrete slab inside a building under construction), backsights, checks, then stakes offsets, grades, gridlines, wall lines, sleeves and hangers; writes cut/fill and station data on lath or slab. Rough ground, mud, traffic, reshores, congested trades.

Reality-capture and aerial topographic mapping: weekly as-built/progress scans of a building or structure with a survey-grade scanner, and open-area topographic/volume mapping of earthwork sites, stockpiles and corridors flown with a mapping drone, then georeferenced and delivered as surfaces or point clouds.

Ground topographic, detail, as-built and control surveys with total station or GNSS rover: technician occupies control, resects or backsights, then identifies and shoots coded features — manhole rims and inverts, curb returns, utility appurtenances, breaklines, benchmarks — including under tree canopy, in traffic corridors and inside occupied facilities.

Boundary/cadastral fieldwork: recover and interpret physical evidence (iron pins, monuments, fences, occupation) on private and rural parcels using metal detector and shovel, set up over found monuments, run traverse and measure ties with theodolite/total station and prism, record in data collector.

Deformation monitoring and repeat control observation at an institution-controlled facility (tunnel, dam, mine, rail corridor, plant): a total station is installed on a bracket or pillar and observes arrays of prisms on the structure on a fixed cycle; results logged, adjusted and alarmed.

instances.label: Ground topographic / existing-conditions survey of a developed site or street corridor: technician occupies control, walks the site with a GNSS RTK rover and robotic total station, shoots and feature-codes buildings, curbs, pavement, driveways, trees, poles, drainage and sanitary structures (including dipping inverts inside manholes), and paint-marked utilities, working around traffic, parked cars, fences, vegetation and private yards.

Boundary / ALTA / cadastral field survey: searching for and recovering existing monuments (iron pipes, rebar, nails, stones) with metal detector and shovel under sod, brush, asphalt or debris, tying found evidence and locating improvements, fences and encroachments on private parcels and rural land.

UAV photogrammetry / LiDAR mapping of large open areas: subdivisions, earthwork sites, quarries, landfills, stockpiles and road corridors. Technician plans and launches an RTK/PPK mapping flight (or a docked drone flies on schedule), producing a georeferenced point cloud, DSM and orthomosaic of terrain and structures.

Active construction-site and building as-built / progress location survey: repeated laser-scan capture of installed structure, MEP and interior conditions (and site surfaces) on a live jobsite with moving trades, temporary barriers, stairs and clutter, delivering registered point clouds compared against the BIM/design model.

Underground survey: as-built mapping of mine stopes, drifts, tunnels, shafts and sewer/pipeline interiors — GPS-denied, dark, dusty, unsupported or confined spaces, delivering 3D point clouds tied to the mine or municipal coordinate system.

Hydrographic / bathymetric survey: locating underwater features, channel bottoms, shoals, reservoir or harbor beds and bridge scour using single/multibeam sonar with GNSS positioning from a survey vessel on open water.

Congested or rough outdoor stakeout: urban infill lots, building corners next to existing structures, utility trenches, curb-and-gutter, sloped or muddy ground, brush and spoil piles, material laydown. Rod must be worked into tight, obstructed spots, sometimes offset or extended, with frequent line-of-sight breaks.

Roadway and street corridor layout/pre-marking on paved surfaces: holding the target at alignment stations, pavement-marking points and ROW offsets within a work zone under traffic control, wearing high-vis, moving between passing vehicles.

Topographic and as-built data collection where the technician chooses each point in the field: setting the rod tip on top of curb, invert of a pipe, base of a utility pole, edge of pavement, grade breaks, tree trunks, building corners, in grass, ditches and slopes, responding to radio direction from the instrument operator.

Boundary/control retracement and differential leveling: occupying found monuments (iron pins, nails, brass discs) and traverse points in rural, wooded, brushy terrain or urban streets, plus holding a graduated level rod plumb on benchmarks and turning points around a level loop.
